speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of personal privilege in regard to an incorrect report in a Canadian Press dispatch of March 5, of a speech I made in this house on March 4, about the Hudson bay route. The dispatch, as used in certain western papers, notably the Regina Leader Post and the Saskatoon Star Phoenix, quotes me as saying that there never had been any suggestion that the port handle any products other than grain. I have never at any time said anything like that. Not only did I plead in general terms for exports and imports through Hudson bay, but at pages 1007, 1008 and 1010 of Hansard I specifically
named certain commodities other than grain that I considered: suitable as exports, among others wood pulp, cattle, poplar wood, feeds; and as imports, woollen goods and coal from the maritimes and diesel engines from England.
This is an unfortunate error; the fact that the speech was not mentioned here in the east and that the reports of it were garbled before being sent to the west might give rise to suspicions not justified by the facts. I hope it will be corrected.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL TRADE CONFERENCE-EMERGENCY POWERS LEGISLATION-EASTER RECESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon.
friend's question gives me an opportunity to touch on an even larger matter, namely the business of the house, and how we are tc get through with it.
As hon. members know, at the beginning of the session the government indicated that it wished priority given to all measures relating to the extension of the national emergency transitional powers, and if possible to have the debate on the address postponed for a short time on that account. The first two weeks were taken up with a discussion of the emergency measures. Then the debate on the address was continued. That debate thus far has taken altogether, I think, two weeks. There was a request, similar to the one which my hon. friend the member for Rosetown-Biggar has made, by another hon. gentleman, the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Gray-don), that time be allowed for the consideration of Canada's participation in the making of the treaties with Germany and Austria. That took up one day. We are now faced with the fact that we have a very short time left between now and the end of the month at which time the emergency transitional powers act ceases to be in force. The government must in every way seek to protect the situation it is faced with in considering how these powers can be extended for the time that in the public interest is absolutely necessary. For this reason, after very careful consideration, the cabinet has come to the decision that we must ask the house to allow us to give precedence and priority to this emergency legislation, that it must have the right of way and from now on be considered before everything else because of the appalling situation that would arise should it happen that some of the powers that are needed to run on into the new fiscal year had not been secured in time.
Yesterday a question came up about the Easter recess. Since that time the whips have met together and I understand that all parties in the. house wish to have a longer rather than a shorter period for a vacation. I believe there are individual members in some of the parties who prefer it otherwise, but I am told that the majority in every party would prefer to have the Easter recess from April 2 to April 14 rather than for the shorter period. In deference to the wishes of all parties in the house I would now ask the Clerk to have a resolution placed on the order paper that when this house adjourns on Wednesday, April 2, it shall stand adjourned until Monday, April 14. That means that the early part of April will not be available for the discussion of these emergency measures. That will bring us to the middle of April before that discussion could be proceeded with. In these circumstances the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) before the end of the present week will have to indicate to the house how he hopes to be able to make sure that the necessary legislation will be enacted in a manner that will, as I say, protect the whole situation.
The government is anxious to have as many subjects debated as possible and questions will arise from time to time which will be important, but if this session is to be concluded before the autumn, we shall have to clear the decks of emergency legislation so that we can get on with the other business of the session. I am sure that more progress will be made [DOT]in the end if we take this one important matter of emergency legislation and stay with it until we have cleared the slate of the various measures relating thereto. For this reason the government wishes to have the house proceed from now on-and I will have a word to say about the word "now" in a moment- with the emergency legislation.
I have said, from now on. There was an agreement among the leaders of the parties that an effort would be made to bring the debate on the address to a conclusion today. It was an agreement made of course with the understanding that no leader can speak for his whole following, that unless the following is willing to fall in line with an agreement of the kind it may not be possible to carry it out. I am told that there are a number of hon. members who still wish to speak in the debate on the address, that up to the present there are twelve whose names have been handed in, and there may be more as the debate proceeds. That means that if we are to get through with the debate today in accordance with the agreement, the speeches will have to
Inquiries of the Ministry

be short. Should they run beyond the hoyr of eleven, perhaps the house would give its consent to sitting until twelve this evening to see if we cannot finish by that time, with the understanding that the vote itself would be postponed until tomorrow but would be taken tomorrow afternoon. If, however, the debate is not concluded today, if the house does not give its consent to having the debate concluded if necessary by continuing to sit until midnight today, with the understanding that the vote be taken tomorrow, we shall just have to proceed tomorrow in accordance with the agreement made some days ago among the leaders of the different parties, and continue with the emergency measures, allowing the continuance of the debate on the address to stand over to another time.
In the circumstances I hope it may be possible for hon. members to find some way to accommodate the wishes I believe of the house as a whole by bringing the speeches in the debate on the address to a conclusion today. In this connection may I point out that the United Kingdom parliament has found it necessary to adopt two practices which up to the present at any rate we have not adopted in this house. One is the use of closure. As applied in the parliament of the United Kingdom, closure has come to be regarded as a natural and necessary method of proceeding to get through with the amount of business that has to be transacted. In this parliament we have sought to avoid the introduction of closure, and I hope it may not be necessary for some time to come.
The other practice is that with respect to debates that are likely to take any length of time, no matter how important they are, there is an agreement made between the leaders of the parties as to the number of days the debate shall take. The number of days having been agreed upon, the amount of time to be allotted to the different parties is also agreed to. It is then left to the whips of the parties to arrange among the parties themselves what particular speakers are to have the preference or to speak for the party in the time which is allotted; but the minute the time agreed upon is reached, speaking in the debate ends. We have not adopted that practice as yet. If we can get agreement among the leaders, and have the followers support it, for a definite time for a debate, then we may not have to take the further step, but if we cannot reach these matters by agreement something will have to be done in the way of amending the rules so as to make possible the conclusion of debates on particular subjects within a definite time.

Mr. Speaker, the election in Pontiac brought great hopes in the hearts of a little group of men forming what is called the Union of Electors. At long last, a voice expressing their beliefs was to be heard in this august chamber of the Canadian parliament. Every one was living in impatient and joyful expectation.
In the first days of the session, a rumour spread in parliamentary circles. The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Caouette) was to speak on the speech from the throne and woe to the Liberal party.
Eventually, he did address the house. His first speech caused some sensation. He had selected from his electoral speeches those passages which had attracted most the favours and the applause of his electors. The speech was clearly meant for the hustings. The hon. member had nothing original to offer; he repeated well known themes and he had the rare merit of being called to order twice in succession. After all, one should not expect too much from a maiden speech.
Then some of his most fanciful statements having been challenged by the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand) it was once more rumoured that the hon. member for Pontiac was to speak, this time on the social credit amendment. He spoke once again last night, but I doubt very much that this time his speech, adorned with a picture of the hon. member on the title-page, will be distributed throughout the province. He reiterated these doleful denunciations of the past and made dire predictions for the future. The remedies boil down to empty suggestions and impractical generalizations. People live miserably in a land of plenty. The bankers who control money and credit are responsible. Social Credit can produce abundance for everyone by reforming the monetary system and controlling credit.

Such materialism does not make abstraction of the spiritual factor; on the contrary, since it contends to be a complete philosophy of life; first it aims to satisfy every physical need and the spirit fulfils itself in physical surfeit.
This distinguishes their materialism from ordinary materialism which denies the existence of the soul; it is even more dangerous since it is less crude.
According to the concepts of social credit, society is primarily dependent on the, economic fact of consumption; man is essentially a consumer of the products of his labour. It is that activity which distinguishes him from other creatures of nature.
All his other activities not only presuppose consumption but they are entirely dependent thereon. It is consumption which determines those activities including purely spiritual pursuits. Consumption is achieved by means of purchasing power, by means of money. The hon. member for Pontiac expressed himself as follows:
For the Canadian people and for any one of us, having security and freedom means having buying power. When we have money we also have security and freedom. Without money we have neither.
It must be noted that this is a direct cause to effect relation. Purchasing power, that is money, determines not only the economic relations between human beings but the fundamental relations of social life. Like any epicurean, social credit abhors work and seeks by every possible means to reduce it to the bare necessity. I wish to refer in this connection to the speech delivered last session by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Kuhl) in which he denounced the obligation to work.

I did not intend to start my speech in that tone, Mr. Speaker, because I did not know I was to follow my hon. friend; but I have so started. I desire to be constructive in what I have to say; in fact the amendment that has been proposed by the group sitting in this corner of the house is designed to put forth constructive proposals. I should like to keep our debates on that high plane if possible. I think there is perhaps a little too much of knocking the government without at the same time offering some adequate proposals which they might at least try. I saw a little poem in the Canadian Social Crediter which expresses my view. It is entitled "The Quarrelsome Trio", and goes like this:
When you hark to the voice of the knocker; As you list to his hammer fall.
Remember the fact that the knocking act Requires no brains at all.
The second and third stanzas deal with the growler and the kicker, and since we want to get through by twelve o'clock tonight I shall omit those. The last stanza reads:
The knocker, the growler, the kicker,
Fault finders large and small;
What do they need for each day's deed?
No brains, no sense-just gall.
I believe the vote on the amendment we have proposed will show where each party in this house stands in respect to the financial position which has developed in Canada over the years. I wonder where the Liberal party stands in respect to a financial policy, or in respect to anything. The other day the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made a

The Address-Mr. Hanse.ll
speech, I think to his own party, in which he said he was going to follow a middle of the road policy. Evidently he stands in the middle of the road. A short time before that I read several times in the press that the Prime Minister had declared himself against third parties. I want you, Mr. Speaker, to put together those two suggestions by the Prime Minister. He wants to stand in the middle of the road, yet he does not believe in third parties. Well, even though he only believes in a second party, where is that second party to stand?
It is all right for the Prime Minister to say he is following a middle of the road policy, but I am certain history will prove that is not the case. Sometimes he is on the left side of the road, and then suddenly he moves to the right side. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) says he must be tight. Well, I don't know about being tight; all I know is that he wabbles from one side of the road to the other whenever it suits his political convenience. I wish the Liberal party would declare once and for all where they stand. They are either following the proposals of one world philosophy, communism, or they are following the only other world philosophy, democracy. It must be one or the other. There is no middle of the road today; let us not fool ourselves on that; you are on either one side or the other. So let the Liberal party declare openly whether they are for one philosophy or the other, and act accordingly.
Since our amendment was moved, one or two press articles and news dispatches have been sent out concerning it. One news article states that the amendment is rather nebulous, following our nebulous theories. Let us look at it again; surely it cannot be so hard to understand a thing of this kind:
A.	The return to parliament of complete and effective control of Canada's financial policy.
There is nothing nebulous or vague about that, and surely it is desirable.
B.	The use of the national credit to meet at least some of the financial requirements for essential services . . .
Certainly there is nothing nebulous about that.
. . . and, as a guarantee that this country shall not again be subjected to financial depression...
Surely there is nothing wrong with that, and nothing nebulous about it. It does not take more than a grade 4 or grade 5 standing to understand it.
. . . to make available to each and all Canadian citizens a proper portion of purchasing power which shall not first pass through the usual channels of industry . . .
Nothing hard to understand about that, is there?
. . . this on a basis calculated to maintain a balance between effective purchasing power in the hands of consumers and the aggregate of the prices of goods available for sale.
Is there anything difficult to understand about that? A man comes along with a balance. On one side he places a pound of butter, on the other a pound weight. Is there anything hard to understand about that?
Where did he get the butter?

It need not be butter; take something else. There is nothing hard to understand about that. So if we say you put your total production in terms of prices on one side of the scale and the total amount of money required to balance it on the other, is there anything hard to understand about that? That is what the resolution says. What we claim is that there is not sufficient purchasing power coming out of the usual courses of production to buy back all the goods. What we want is an additional amount of purchasing power. There is nothing hard or difficult to understand in that.
Another article suggested that it was our usual pie in the sky amendment. I am not going to say very much about pie in the sky; all I am going to say is that the pie we have is right here on the ground, right here on earth. I challenge that gentleman to write an article proving that our amendment is pie in the sky-
He was pie-eyed.

-and that he was not pie-eyed.
I said a little while ago that there is a need for every hon. member of this house to understand a few things in respect to the present system of money. We hear it said quite often that they do not understand social credit. What they do not understand is the present system of money management. The other day when the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) was speaking I listened with a great deal of interest to what he said. It would not have been so alarming if he had confined his remarks to his own responsibility, but he said, and I quote from page 160 of Hansard:
We of this group are convinced that the only way in which we can obtain and maintain a higher standing of liviflg in Canada is by higher production and more equitable distribution. Until we take the necessary steps to obtain that higher production and more equitable distribution we cannot hope to raise our living standards.
The Address-Mr. Hansell

I am not finding fault with that, but he went on:
Our whole policy is designed for that purpose.
That is the C.C.F.

That is the C.C.F. party. The hon. member continued:
Today we see evidence of the failure of free enterprise to do these things. Let me quote to you, sir, from an editorial in the Winnipeg Tribune. "With $3,477 million tied up in savings deposits Canadian bankers are able to get only $1,438 million out at work in tile form of ^current loans."
Apparently our free enterprise system has lost its enterprise. It has come to the point where it is dependent more and more upon government, upon protection, upon other forms of subsidy, to make it not free but very much under control.
What the hon. member was saying is that as there is a certain amount of idle money on deposit in the banks, the banks have not lent that money. He assumes at the outset that the banks lend their depositors' money. He does not know, and apparently that would carry through to his group, the way the present money system works. Evidently they do not know the rudimentary principle that banks do not lend their depositors' money. The money that is lent by banks is freshly created money, money that is created by a stroke of a pen, money which becomes an expansion of credit, which goes out in the form of loans and which becomes the depositors' money. Sometimes even intelligent people get the cart .before the horse. Some years ago I was debating here when an hon. member on the Liberal side of the house rose to ask a question. I said to him, "Will my hon. friend tell me where money actually comes from?" The hon. member said, "Oh, well, I earn it". That was his answer to my question as to where money comes from. He was a member of parliament. Of course I know that it does not take brains to become a member of parliament, but I suppose the people of the country think that members of parliament are of average intelligence. Yet this member when I asked him where money actually comes from said, "I earn it". He must still believe what my leader said, that storks drop babies down the chimney.
Not long after that I was talking to a medical doctor. I think it can be assumed that a medical doctor would have considerable intelligence, because he probably went to university for a number of years. My friend who said that railroads distribute our production is a doctor, and he must have some intelligence. I asked this doctor that very same question: "Where does money come from; how does it get into existence? How

is it born? Where does it come from?- because you do not pick it out of the air." He said, "Oh, well, I have a wheat field out here; that is money." I said, "Do you mean that dollar bills grow on the ends of the stalks?" "Oh, no," he said, "of course not; I sell my wheat and the grain buyer gives me the money." I said, "Where would the grain buyer get the money?" He replied, "Oh, well, well, well, well." That was his answer.
I remember asking another man this same question. He was not a member of parliament and he was not a doctor; he was just a farmer who was reaching the old age pension age. He used to say that he did not know very much because he had gone only to grade four, that all he had ever learned was learned when he was ploughing behind the horses or sitting on the tractor. I said to that old gentleman, "Where would you say money comes from?" The old fellow closed his eyes and said, "Well, let me see; I guess the banks must make it." That farmer was closer to the truth than was the member of parliament or the doctor.
Coming down on the train the other day I met a man in the parlour car. We introduced ourselves and I discovered that he was the head of a million dollar corporation. He asked me about social credit in Alberta, and it was not long before I found that he thought that the banks lent their depositors' money. One of the first principles we have to know is that money is a creature of law. The law permits the merchant or chartered banks to issue that money from the end of a fountain pen. Some hon. members may still think that this is just so much nonsense. I refer them to the report of the proceedings of the banking and commerce committee of 1939, when Mr. Graham Towers, governor of the Bank of Canada, was on the stand and being questioned by Mr. Landeryou. Mr. Towers replied to a question-I shall not read the whole thing- by saying:
A government can find money in three ways: By taxation, or they might find it by borrowing the savings of the people-
As was done by way of victory loans, raising money that was already in existence.

or they might find it by action which is allied with an expansive monetary policy, that is, borrowing which creates additional money in the process.
The only way in which money can possibly go out is by way of loans from the bank, which is a fresh creation: and conversely, when a bank loan is paid, the money is destroyed, wiped out of existence-believe me. Now I turn to page 238 of the same report. Again Mr. Towers is giving evidence, and I quote

The Address-Mr. Harwell
him because surely he should know what he is talking about, and he does. I have listened to him.
Q. Now, if the government went to the bank with $1,000,000 in bonds there would be an increase of $1,000,000 in the amount of money in the hands of the people in the form of deposits? A. Assuming that no other change had taken place in the bank's position at that time, yes.
Q. In other words, when the $1,000,000 worth of bonds is presented to the bank a million dollars of new money or the equivalent is created? A. Again assuming that there is no decrease in its other investments or loans.
Q. I mean at the time, at the moment. A. Yes.
Q. It is a fact that a million dollars of new money is created? A. That is right. Of course, governments should not always go to banks in that connection; they should sell their bonds to investors.
Q. Yes. Now, the same thing holds true when the municipality or the province goes to a bank?
A. Or an individual borrower.
I skip some for the sake of brevity, and quote from a little further down on the same page:
Q. What is the proper way? Is the proper way this, that when I borrow $100 from the bank as a private citizen the bank makes a bookkeeping entry and there is a $100 increase in the deposits of that bank, in the total deposits of that bank? A. Yes.
I will give just one other quotation, from page 287 of the same report. Mr. Towers is being questioned by Mr. McGeer:
Q. But there is no question about it that the banks do create that medium of exchange? A. That is right. That is what they are there for.
Q. That is what they are there for and that is what they do. A. Yes, they do.
Q. And they issue that form of medium of exchange when they purchase securities or make loans? A. That is banking business, just in the same way that a steel plant makes steel.
Q. So that we are clear on this point that our merchant banks do create and issue 88 per cent of the money medium of exchange in common use in Canada today? That is correct, is it? A. Roughly.
"Roughly" does not apply to whether the practice is right or not, but to the figure 88 per cent. It is well for us to understand that one thing or we shall never understand the present financial system, let alone social credit proposals. When I go to the bank to borrow $100, I give my signed note to the banker, the teller puts $100 in figures in my bank pass book, I walk out of the bank and there is $100 more in existence than there was when I walked in. We cannot solve the problems of the day if we do not understand the function and operation of money.
We have heard a great deal in this debate about the need for a planned economy, and I want to deal with that for a moment. My
gorge always rises a little when I hear that term "planned economy." I should like to know in the first place who is going to do the planning.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Who does it now?

The point I am trying to make is that in a free society the less planning we have the better. I am saying something more. When we talk about planners making plans, the principle carries with it the absolute necessity of people having to fit into those plans. Suppose for instance, that a section of our country says:	We are not going
to have the planners tell us what to do; we do not agree with this plan. What would happen then? I heard a prominent speaker, the leader of the C.C.F. in Alberta, in a radio broadcast in that province, attack the premier of Alberta simply because he was not in accord with this constant eager clamour for planning. The leader of the C.C.F. in Alberta said: Look at General Montgomery, look at Churchill', look at General Eisenhower-they had to plan to win the war-how would we ever win a war if we did not plan? That was an excellent illustration, but it was a dead give-away. The only reason why Montgomery and Churchill and Eisenhower and the rest were successful when they planned, was that they had armies, air forces and navies at their command, made up of men who had to obey I heir orders.
And the only reason why we never wron the peace is that we never had anyone to plan that.

What we are saying is ' this, that individuals in the aggregate will do their own planning. They do their own planning now by having sufficient money to buy our goods. I had a school teacher come to me once and say:	We have to plan production. I said, "What do you mean, plan production?" I said, "Here is a furniture manufacturer; does ne have to plan anything?" Does he? In a free society he would not; in a free society he simply offers his goods for sale, and people with money buy them. If they do not like one kind of chesterfield, they will buy another. That is the planning. Therefore the manufacturer says, "I will have to manufacture certain types of goods, because that is what the people want."
That is planning.

It is the money tokens which determine our production. I say, Mr. Speaker, that planning becomes effective only in so far as the people are willing to submit to the plan. But I might say that some of
The Address-Mr. Lacombe

these planners are not only clamouring to plan out own country and our own lives, but they talk in terms of world planning.
Why not take in the universe?

Yes, and rule the Almighty. The greatest plan under heaven is found in the natural order of things, as they were created. Each individual is created a free moral agent. Let the individual plan his own life in peace, in security, and in freedom. This is the difference between social credit and other types of philosophy. Social credit is interested in people, in life and in the individual. The less law, the less control, the less regulation-
Order. I would remind the hon. member that his time has expired.

Thank you very much. You did not need to remind me; I was going to resume my seat. The less law, the less regulation, the less control, the less planning we have, and the more money we have, the better it will be for the people.

Mr. Chairman, the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) includes excellent practical suggestions. The hon. member stresses the importance of Parliament's supremacy over boards that are not responsible to the people. He condemns bureaucracy which, owing to the war, has substituted itself for the representatives of the people. Controls over the production of raw materials required for the development of our home and foreign trades have been imposed by bureaucracy. I wish to be fair and to recognize the useful features of the amendment to the amendment moved by the leader of the Social Credit group. However, like many others, I fear "the redefining and clarifying of the constitutional rights and responsibilities of dominion and provincial governments" as expressed in subparagraph D. of the amendment to the amendment. Indeed, Canada's constitution clearly defines the respective jurisdiction of the provinces and of the Dominion government. Personally. I consider that any amendment to the constitution of the country, in contempt of provincial jurisdiction, would violate rights which have been established and recognized for eighty years. This question of national importance offers more than a financial angle.

It must be borne in mind that provinces have the exclusive right to legislate in matters of education.
Vainly have I scanned this amendment to the amendment for some reservation of this sacred prerogative. Provinces also have the right to legislate when it comes to safeguarding social welfare and, especially in the province of Quebec, when it comes to maintaining our French civil legislation. Let us not forget that confederation itself established autonomous legislature, each with its own jurisdiction which they may exercise within the limits of the constitutional laws governing them. This very law states in what matters provinces may legislate independently from the federal government. Unless some specific reservation is made regarding provincial autonomy, and I find none in this amendment to the amendment, I greatly fear that a new delimitation of powers, without consulting the provinces, or seeking their consent will lead us straight to legislative union. That is a principle I am not prepared to accept. Still less do I agree with the views expressed in this connection by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix). Speaking in this house on March 4 last, he did indeed recommend that provincial governments surrender the collection of succession duties to the federal authorities. Despite all my regard for my hon. colleague's opinions, I say that such a surrender would be a glaring infringement of provincial rights. Furthermore, it would mean relinquishing into the hands of the federal government a jurisdiction which the provinces have assumed since confederation. Besides, the province of Quebec civil code contains a whole chapter on estates and the revised statutes of the same province comprise several chapters on the collection of succession duties. I am opposed to our French civil laws being superseded by federal government jurisdiction. It is supremely unfair to make the provincial premiers responsible for the abuses that might be perpetrated in connection with the estates of rich people. If the safety deposit boxes of the banks hide any degree of dishonesty, the federal government, who have collected income tax since the first world war, should discharge their duty. Indeed, my good friend, the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr LaCroix) admits that the federal government has the exclusive right of supervision over the Canadian banking system. It is therefore the duty of the central government to open these safety deposit boxes to collect any unpaid income tax. Why blame the provincial

The Address-Mr. Skey
premiers for an existing evil for which they are not in the least responsible? I am sorry that extremely unfair statements have been levelled, in this house, at the leaders of the provinces forming the Canadian confederation. What is to result from such conduct? The old proverb still holds true:	He who sows the
wind shall reap the whirlwind.
Canada participated in the last war in order to protect Christianity, the rights of minorities, freedom and justice. Any government willing to trample on the rights of minorities through the violation of provincial autonomy would ignore the heroism of our soldiers and the war aims of the united nations. Let us not add to the affront that is now directed against us by the Moscow conference, in showing contempt for Canada. That was to be expected. During five years. I have constantly told the government that if we relied on the gratitude of Soviet Russia in the preparation of peace treaties, we would be sure to be disappointed. That is the result of our numerous sacrifices on behalf of a country which has showed its gratitude by conducting espionage activities and creating communist cells in Canada. A few hours ago, a priest and a member of a religious order who were on the staff of one of the leading educational institutions in my constituency, the Laval College in St. Vincent de Paul, were stabbed in the very city of Montreal. It is said that the man guilty of that double crime is 30 years old and that he believes in a doctrine which he expounds as follows: "I wanted to take vengeance on all those who practise the Catholic religion".
How can we not dread the election of a communist member in Montreal-Cartier on March 31 next? Drastic measures should have been taken to prevent such an election. The only legal course to follow was to outlaw the communist party in Canada.
Hear. hear.

The government did not hesitate to take such a stand at the beginning of the war. I then supported them most heartily. Let them outlaw that party. The government will thus render a very great service to honest people, in protecting them against scoundrels of every description. There is a limit to tolerance, especially when it works to the detriment of religion and the nation. Since the amendment to the amendment deals with constitutional rights and the responsibilities of the dominion and provincial governments, I must say that there is another aspect of the rights of minorities which I wish to discuss briefly. Redistribution of electoral divisions was only possible through 83166-81
an amendment to the constitution. In that redistribution we should, in none of the provinces of confederation, take any action likely to reduce to insignificant proportions the representation of minorities, whatever their origin may be. In no province of Canada are there no minority rights to protect. Finally, I wish that my province may increase its representation in the House of Commons, but on the distinct condition that its influence should always be based on truth and justice.

Mr. Speaker, I am another member of this house who felt that he must rise to speak in the interests of people and of freedom in the same way that my hon. friend from the Social Credit party (Mr. Hansell) has just done. But before I turn to the three questions which I believe concern Canada most, those of taxes, controls and security, may I take the house back to 1945 just to clear up one small point which was left hanging in the air at that time. It is a question that has been before the Canadian people for upwards of two years now. I refer to the manner in which Canada's war assets have been dealt with, and I wish to quote first the words of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) spoken on March 20, 1946, as reported at page 114 of Hansard. Speaking in the debate on the speech from the thrcne, he said:
Rather a significant thing has happened recently. The United States government has tried several methods of disposing of war assets. About three months ago they scrapped all their disposal procedures and set up the exact machinery which we are using in Canada, stating quite frankly that they did so because they thought our machinery worked where theirs did not.
The minister went on to say:
Therefore the disposal agency in the United States is now the war assets corporation, exactly the same name and exactly the same type of organization that we are using here in Canada.
My reason for bringing up that point is that I happened to pick up a United States newspaper a few months ago and I found in it a detailed explanation of how the American people are allowed to buy their surplus war products. This, I believe, is an accurate report of how their surplus products are disposed of in the United States. An advertisement is placed in the press; the goods to be sold are detailed in this advertisement, and their location is given. Then a date is set, allocating a first period of three or four days. During this first period, the first priority, veterans, men and women, of the armed forces, on presentation of their discharge certificates can enter this dump and have first choice, at the

The Address-Mr. Skey

price set, of goods of the United States war assets corporation. Then, when the veterans are disposed of, another date is fixed later than the first when schools, educational institutions, state and municipal bodies can go to the same dump and purchase war assets. A third date is then set on which the general public are allowed to purchase back from the state the goods which they have paid for in taxation.
I should like to contrast that for a moment with what happens in Canada. I suppose every member of this house and many members of the general public as well as businessmen in the country have had the unfortunate and frustrating experience of trying to buy something from War Assets Corporation in Canada. They will know what trouble they must go to and what little they will find in some cases in return, because they find that in this country war assets have sold back to some business organization, or secondary corporation, the goods that the taxpayers have purchased for the use of our military forces. These organizations can then take a second profit from the country on the surplus goods purchased from War Assets.
I wish here today to refute absolutely the statement of the minister of reconstruction as to the similarity between the United States method of dealing with war assets and that of the Canadian government.
I should now like to turn to the three questions of taxes, controls and security. As I see these three, they are to a large extent inter-related. I see them for the most part as a fight between the government and the individual as to who shall spend the individual's money, as to who shall control the individual's destiny, and as a fight by the individual to secure his economic future in this country. If I may give the house one or two illustrations of this, I should like to turn first to taxation.
When the budget was presented last year, as members of the house will remember, there were words in it to the effect that the purchasing power of the people must be siphoned off because there were insufficient goods and high incomes. At that time, Mr. Speaker, you will remember that wo endeavoured to modify the government's taxation policy, because we believed that a less drastic taxation policy would allow corporations and individuals to stimulate business by both production and purchasing. As we have now seen, from the surpluses produced by the budget last year, it was a crushing burden for the Canadian people to bear. With regard to taxation this year, we find that women are no longer seeking employment

in business such as confectionery manufacture, laundries, bakeries, cleaning establishments and any number of other businesses, which are hard pressed to maintain their services and their output of goods because the government has seen fit to pronounce only a $250 exemption for married women. These women who have worked through the war years, who are required now to increase Canada's production, to combat inflation, to help the needy in Britain and Europe, find that their husbands are penalized by the fact that they are at work. I wish to say with all the force at my command that this one clause in the budget of last year must be changed. It is injurious to the economic life of Canada. The taxation exemption of married women must be increased.
This excessive taxation has in other ways made the lot of the white-collar worker exceptionally hard. He has been faced with a fixed income, rising prices and rising costs and is beset by many difficulties. It has also affected the wage-earner in that he has lost much of his incentive because, as soon as the taxation deductions begin to come out of his weekly pay envelope, he begins to wonder whom he is working for-his wife, his family, himself or the federal government.
We have seen many cases where difficulties arose from controls. I am going to quote only one today and I acknowledge that I tread upon dangerous political ground when I speak of rent control; but I would speak especially for one part of our population, namely, the aged people who own property and are unable to obtain possession of it. I know of cases in the city from which I come, in which older people who had rented property at the time of the freezing of rents have for many years been unable to obtain possession of this property. Some of them are approaching the pensionable age. They are living perhaps in one room, cooking over a gas burner, and the small amount of security of a home which they had provided for themselves in their old age is being denied them. I would plead with this government especially for some relaxation of the property controls in the way in which they affect old people and prevent them from occupying the homes they have purchased for their old age.
As an example of what can be done, I should like to cite to the house the case of the compulsory war savings certificates, which were undertaken by the British government during the war in order to obtain the necessary revenue. As a matter of fact, I myself hold compulsory war savings certificates for a few pounds and I do not expect they will be paid within the next twenty years. But the

The Address-Mr. Skey
British government has seen fit to pay compulsory savings certificates to people over sixty-five years of age, because they realize that those are the people who need help. Those are the people who are coming to the time in life when their physical strength is perhaps failing them a little. They want help; they want shelter, and they want to enjoy some of the fruits of their savings. I would say to this government that they must revise their rent controls in some way to take care of special cases. I know it is true that the landlord has been beset by rising costs, heavy maintenance and repair work as well as heavy taxation, and at times he has been saddled with inconsiderate tenants; but that condition we must consider to some extent as an offshoot of the war and one which I hope will soon correct itself.
I should now like to turn to price control for a moment, and deal with one phase of it only. I wish to quote from the headlines of the Globe and Mail of last fall; under dateline of October 29, we have a report, presumably official, from the wartime prices and trade board. The heading is:
Moderate ceiling rises seen for some goods; may not hit foodstuffs
Farther down in the article we find these words:
Only to a slight extent, if at all, however, will any adjustments affect food prices.
Then just four or five days later, Mr. Speaker, the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, speaking on the national network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, said exactly the opposite. The headline reads:
Food price rise certain once controls lifted, Reminder from Gordon
So we have a considerable amount of confusion in the mind of the general public, as is illustrated by just these two quotations. In one case they are told that prices will not rise; then the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board goes on the air and tells them that prices will rise. I recall plainly hearing the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) in this house last summer, tired and harassed as he was by the industrial relations committee, saying time and again that you could not have price control without a measure of wage control. He practically opened and closed that committee with those very words. Well, we have had wage control lifted, and now we are wondering just how long the government will continue to try to fool the people into believing they can actually control prices, because the housewives of Canada know the government have failed in what they tried to do.
83166-81J
Yet they maintain an expensive inspection and enforcement body all across the country. If you talk to the people who spend the money, the women, in spite of Mr. Gordon spending five hours on the air, or whatever time it was, they know that he has failed in his mission. It is about time the government admitted it and did something about it.
I need not read any more quotations in that connection. I feel that this price control farce is one of the worst things that has ever been foisted on the Canadian people. To go for a moment into the realm of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), one bad feature about it is this. The announcements made by the government are confusing and frightening to the marginal people of this country, the men and women who are struggling along trying to raise families, with perhaps a few dollars over one week and a few dollars short the next week. Every time the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board or one of his minions goes on the air or makes these announcements these people become more and more fearful at these repressive measures. I am sure the people of Canada would prefer the facts.
There is only one other matter I should like to mention, and I shall do so briefly; that is security. The men and women of Canada who are being taxed so heavily and controlled and decontrolled by the government in this frenzied fashion, all have in mind their own personal security. If the majority were to pass judgment on this government I believe they would say, "We prefer to keep a larger part of our income and be the arbiters as to how we shall spend it." I think they feel they would rather make provision for their own future security than trust it to the government. One way in which this could be done would be to have started a national contributory pension plan, so that young men who entered an industry which perhaps did not have a pension plan of its own would be able to contribute to a government scheme of this kind. That would relieve the state of the necessity of caring for them in later years as old age pensioners and give them a feeling of security for the future. Further in that connection I should like to quote again, because I desire to have it appear in what I have said today, what was said by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) on March 7 of this year, appearing at page 1114 of Hansard. There the hon. member spoke in support of Canadian businessmen. I have been dealing with these matters on an individual basis, but the hon. member dealt with the case of the businessman much better than I could have done. He said:
The Address-Mr. Tucker

. . . the businessmen of this country have been pushed around, not only during the war but since, as though thev were enemies of the state. Success on the part of the individual is becoming a subject of deprecation. To many bureaucrats a businessman, however honest he may be, is an object of suspicion and in many cases a parasite to be denounced. The honest businessman-
Here I would add the employer of labour, the man who risks his capital, the man who uses his initiative, his brains and his scientific genius.
-no less than the farmer and the worker and other citizens, should be entitled to fair and equitable treatment.
When I began, Mr. Speaker, I took as my main approach the fight by the individual against the government for control of his own life, as long as he does not trespass against his neighbour. I have endeavoured to show that the individual has been denied security because of excessive taxation and hobbling controls. I conclude with the remark with which I opened: that I as an individual, and I know we as a party, stand for the people and their freedom from control by government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to follow the hon. member who has just spoken, except to this extent. He said that, in his opinion, price control was the greatest farce ever imposed on the Canadian people.

speechtext: Oh, keep quiet.

I do not wish to go into the Veterans Land Act at any great length because this matter was covered very well and completely by the right hon. minister in his presentation to the house. However, some things have been said and, although I have not the time to deal with them in full, I should like to say a few words in regard to the general picture of the small holdings programme.
The part of this programme that has come under criticism in this house comprises something over 2,600 houses which were built by the Veterans Land Act administration pursuant to a request that they make some contribution to the building shortage. In order to try to help out, they negotiated to build a certain number of houses. They have built between 2,600 and 2,700 houses, but that is only a small part of the whole programme. Up to the end of January, 1947, there were settled by the Veterans Land Act administration 12,023 veterans in full-time farming; 10,308 on small holdings; 417 in commercial fishing; 994 in full-time farming on provincial projects, making a total of 23,742 who have been settled by the Veterans Land Act administration up to the end of last January. Of course it will be seen by the house that 2,600 is only slightly over ten per cent of the total.
I think it will be admitted by all hon. members who have visited these small holdings that the majority of the men on them are well satisfied with the homes they have. At least that expression has been used to me in connection with the ones I have visited. These men realize that they are getting homes that cost them much less than they would have paid if they had got them them-

The Address-Mr. Tucker
*elves outside of the Veterans Land Act and 3pent their reestablishment credit. Under V.L.A. there has been a write-off of $1,400, jnd in some cases they have had the benefit Df the write-off of part of a million dollars which was appropriated to cut down costs where they have been raised by unusual conditions. There has been some criticism of the delay in regard to the Veterans Land Act administration. One reason for the delay was a desire to avoid the mistakes which marked the administration of the soldier settlement department after the first war.

You did not avoid
the mistakes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
We have gone a long
way toward avoiding them. Again that is my . own opinion. I think most people who have studied the situation will agree that the government have gone a long way toward avoiding these mistakes. Therefore it was impossible really to start settling on a large scale until the late fall of 1945. As hon. members know, safe settlement cannot be indulged in during the winter when the ground is covered with snow, so that meant it was really the spring of 1946 before work could be started on any scale. It meant also that so far there has been only one season in which to do this work. As I say, there have been almost 24,000 settled already, which I think is not a bad record thus far.
There has been some criticism of the houses, but I would say that one of the reasons for the difficulty is that which has faced anyone who has tried to build a. house, the shortage of proper materials. Builders working for the Veterans Land Act administration in many cases had to work with inferior building materials. It was never thought that ultimately these houses would not be brought up to specifications, but it was felt that it was better to have houses completed and roofs over the heads of a large number of veterans than to stand upon red tape and refuse to let them go ahead with the building.
That excuse is just as leaky as the roofs of the houses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I wonder that the hon. gentleman says anything in view of his remarks a few minutes ago. That was the attitude in regard to this matter, that it was better to go ahead. It was impossible in some cases to finish the houses to specifications and representations were made that the houses should be opened so that veterans would be able to get shelter. In many cases veterans were permitted to take possession of houses before they were finished and. therefore, before there was any chance to decide what the final cost would be.
I do not know whether my hon. friends would have said that we should have prevented these veterans from taking possession until the houses were fully finished, even though they were habitable and would provide roofs over their heads. I sometimes think they are quite reckless with their criticism.
Nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
It may be nonsense to my hon. friend; he may be an expert in nonsense, but in any event the effect of that criticism was that the contractors who had agreed to their houses being taken possession of before they were finished found themselves advertised all over the country as having done a poor job when it was understood that they would have to go back and finish the job. They now do not want to give possession of houses until fully finished because they will be held up all over the country as having done a poor job. The result is the department is having difficulty in getting possession of houses before they are fully finished. There is a feeling now that, in view of the criticism which has been indulged in, the only safe policy is to wait until the houses are absolutely finished before possession is granted.
The Address-Mr. Tucker
Will my hon. friend permit a question? Will he say that there was nothing wrong with the houses built for the veterans of this country?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The government has never said that. If my hon. friend will just contain himself a moment he will hear what I have to say. We had to use inferior materials and surely that fact will penetrate into my hon. friend's head. I just finished saying that at no time was there any thought that this obligation should not be accepted and these houses be finished according to specifications. But I said it was felt that it was important to give these boys roofs over their heads as quickly as possible, and I think that should have been taken into consideration. As soon as materials can be got to bring these houses up to specifications, they will be brought up to specifications. speechtext: I do not mind questions as long as I am given enough time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I said that this criticism should have taken account of what was being done. I said that the effect of criticism which did not take that fact into account, which did not give credit to the contractors for having let people into their houses before they were finished, was making them afraid to do that now. Had hon. members risen in their places and said that they realized the houses were not finished, that they realized the government had let people take possession before the houses were ready; had they asked for assurance that ultimately the houses would be brought up to specifications as soon as materials could be obtained, nobody would have found any fault whatever.
What about the sites?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I do not intend to take up a whole lot of time to deal with the question of sites. The very basis of this plan was that it should be agricultural land from which a part of the veteran settler's income would come to sustain himself. It was a land settlement scheme, not an urban housing scheme.

It was never intended in the first place that it should be an urban housing scheme. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) complained of the drainage on Lulu island. To complain because some water runs onto the land of a man who is supposed to be going into farming is not fair criticism. The drainage there was also under the control of one of the most competent drainage authorities in Canada.
Was the same authority responsible for the drainage at Braefoot?
Ducks in the cellar.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. There are too many interruptions. There cannot be intelligent discussion with so many interruptions. Questions can be asked only with the permission of the hon. member who has the floor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
In reply to the interjection in regard to Braefoot, in spite of the fact that this administration went somewhat beyond the original intention of the act and engaged in building which was very close to an urban character and actually built at Braefoot, it has not sought to evade responsibility even in that regard. We have said that drainage will be put in as quickly as it can be put in. I am sure hon. members realize that a good job really has been done in providing these 2,700 homes and giving possession as quickly as possible to the veteran. There have been a few defects in workmanship and in materials in some cases, but these defects will be made good at the expense of the public as quickly as possible, and where the contractor is to blame he will be expected to make good. Certainly if that is all hon. members wished to say, they could have said it without suggesting that in some way there had been some terrible breakdown of this whole plan of settlement. There is nothing in the whole plan of which this administration needs to be ashamed. It is wide open to inspection. This administration believes that it has done a good job for a veteran. The veteran who has a house under this scheme knows he is much better off than he would have been had he had to go out like the forty thousand other veterans who have done so and buy a house with his own resources.
I wish to deal for a moment with the question of immigration. I think most of us feel that we are in possession of one of the richest areas on the earth's surface. We are in possession of half of a rich continent, and it is not the proper attitude for us to take, in the present state of world affairs, to say that we

The Address-Mr. Tucker
are going to bar out of that area large numbers of homeless people who would like to come and make their homes here, particularly the relatives of those who came here and laid the foundations for our country, pioneered it and helped to build it up to the country it is today. They now see their relatives in the old lands from which they came in danger of losing their lives, and they say to us that they would like to be able to give them protection and asylum in this dominion. I would say this to the government in that regard. There has been an extension of the terms upon which people can enter this country, and I appreciate that very much, but some of these extensions should, I think, be much, further extended. From amongst the refugees and displaced persons in Europe anybody in this country should be free to bring in a relative and that relative's family. For example, a man might be willing to come to Canada and work as a farm labourer, or he may be needed in mining, lumbering or the logging industry in this country. To say to such a man, you can come here but you must leave your wife and your family over in Europe with its present unsettled conditions, I say that it is not right to offer to take a man in but ask him to leave his wife and family over there. Our government should not be a party to any policy that is based on such a separation of families, particularly the relatives of those who have laid the foundations of our country, pioneered and built it up to what it is today.
In regard to this whole question of immigration it is generally admitted that we shall need immigrants and the we should let them in, but some say that we should go about this in a slow and careful manner. There seems to be the idea that if we go about it very slowly and take in only a few immigrants each year we shall always be able to get the numbers we want, but with conditions as they are in Europe today I venture to suggest that several of these countries from whom in past years we drew some of our best immigrants will not permit their people to leave their shores. I doubt whether the Scandinavian countries will permit their people to leave their shores in any great numbers, and I believe the same is true of Great Britain herself. I am satisfied from past experience that the nations behind the iron curtain, no matter how much those people may want to leave the control of the Soviet, will not be allowed to leave those countries, and let it not be forgotten that we got some of our best settlers from the Ukraine, Poland and some other countries that are now wholly or partly under the control of the Soviet.
So that the situation today is this. There are about 800,000 people, exactly the kind of people who have helped to build up this country, living in camps in Europe today under terrible conditions and they do not want to go back under the control of the Soviet. They are asking for a chance to find a home in the new world, and we urge that when they have relatives here, they should be permitted to come here, even if we have at one time to take in more than we would take in on an ordinary immigration basis. It is a question of either taking them now and saving their lives or they will be lost to us and be forced back where they fear to go. If we take these people in we shall be taking in settlers who have already demonstrated their loyalty and devotion to the cause of freedom. They have picked themselves as desirable immigrants for Canada by virtue of the fact that they are in these camps. The fact they are there shows they are against totalitarianism, against communism, and so on. I urge the government, with all the strength I have, to adopt a policy which will permit a reasonable number of these people to come in as soon as possible. The first step which I urge should be taken is that relatives of those in this country should be admitted at once.
I should like to tell this house about one thing that has pleased me more than anything else since I came to Ottawa to attend this parliament. A delegation waited on the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) in regard to this question of immigration. It showed the good will and the unity which prevails in this country in regard to this matter, which is not only an economic matter and a political matter but a matter of Christianity and humanity. On that delegation on which I had the honour of accompanying the Prime Minister there were represented all the Lutheran churches in Canada. A representative of the Roman Catholics of the prairies, a representative of all the Mennonites, a representative of all the Sudeten refugees, a representative of all the Ukrainians, both Greek Catholics and Greek Orthodox, a representative of the Poles went there in one combined delegation' and said to the Prime Minister: "Our relatives are over there in danger. We ask you, w'ithout regard to racial origin or religious creed, to allow them to come here to their relatives and find a refuge in this great free country." One of these men said to the Prime Minister: "I never cease to remember that but for the action of your government back in 1938 in admitting us I would not be alive today." Another man said: "I never go to bed at night but what I thank
The Address-Mr. Tucker

God for the privilege of living in this great free country and I want the chance of bringing my relatives here to enjoy the privileges that I have enjoyed."
What did the Prime Minister say?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs

Oh, oh.

speechtext: That may amuse my hon. friends. This is a national question; it is a question of humanity; a question of Christianity; a question on which all parties should join together, and I am making my appeal for the support which all hon. members might care to give to my suggestion.

I come to another matter which is of interest to us, particularly in Saskatchewan. I am sorry that I shall not have time to run over all these subjects with which I wish to deal; therefore I shall do little more than mention some of the points. In regard to the crop failure bonus on the prairies, I would suggest to the government that every possible consideration be given to making the act more flexible. At the present time, if a township has not the requisite yield to bring it within the act a rectangular block of not less than nine sections may be brought into it if it is lying alongside an eligible township. I suggest that that section should be amended to make it more flexible so that it should not necessarily be a rectangular block, or lie alongside an adjacent township, so long as it is within an adjacent township, and that nine sections are too much. If that were made more flexible it would improve the administration of the act.
In regard to prairie farm rehabilitation, I urge most strongly upon the government its extension to the whole province. It should indeed be extended to the whole Dominion of Canada with advantage to the development of the country.
I also wish to commend the government for getting plans ready to spend SI 10 million to

bring under cultivation a million and a half acres of land which cannot be cultivated today because of lack of water. I urge the government to press ahead with its plans as fast as available labour and supplies will permit. This programme which will bring under cultivation a million and a half acres is not an expenditure of money in the ordinary sense; it is an investment in the future development of the country which will pay real dividends in the development of the human resources of our country. As an example of the extent to which it will make a contribution, may I cite the yield in an area in Alberta of 30,000 acres of irrigated land. On these 30,000 acres the sugar beet growers in 1946 received an average return of $150 per acre. This yield was from land which formerly was practically worthless. On all the crops in that area the average yield was S75 an acre.

With regard to barley, the representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture indicated that they would like to see at least $5 paid upon land sown to barley. There have been many arguments about that but I have not time to go into them this afternoon.

speechtext: I am not a member of the government. All I can do is to make my representations.
