speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That may amuse my hon. friends but what is so funny about that?
You have no sense of humour.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I should like to say to the government that I hope it will accept the recommendation. I must say I am doubtful whether $5 an acre will be enough to bring out the production of barley which should be brought out to provide the necessary feed not only for the west but for the eastern part of Canada and British Columbia but it will help.
Why accept it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I notice they also suggested that the freight policy be continued. Under that policy, as hon. members know, $79 million were paid out to January 31, 1947, to subsidize cost of freight on feed grain shipped east and to British Columbia, and $25 million was paid on subsidizing feed grain. Of course tiiat has meant that we could grow more feed grains for live stock and a policy of feeding live stock could be built up in the other parts of Canada.
That brings me to another question, the question of freight rates. It is interesting to note that the assistance given to the cost of shipping of feed grain to British Columbia and to the eastern part of Canada ha3 had such a tremendously beneficial influence upon the building up of the agricultural industry in Ontario. It shows what effect high freight rates have on stultifying and holding back the development of the country. One of the things that holds back the development of our country is the large stretch, the unproductive spread between west of the lakes and east of Winnipeg. There is very little production there and our produce has to be hauled both ways over that stretch. Someone has made a suggestion which might do much more good than studying how to raise rates, and that is to treat that area much as you would treat a river to be crossed, where you provide a bridge at public expense, or perhaps where you provide a canal on which you can haul goods, and do so at the expense of the public. The suggestion is made that if the cost of hauling goods across that unproductive area were paid by the state it would increase development not only in western Canada but in eastern Canada as well. It would increase national development amazingly.
I was pleased at the last meeting of the national Liberal federation that they were definitely opposed to any increase in freight rates. They said that if the railroads had to have more money to carry on, some other method should be adopted than raising the rates. I suggest that the question of paying the cost of hauling goods back and forth across that unproductive stretch might be considered.
It operates very much like a tariff. It costs money for us to fetch goods from eastern
The Address- Mr. Tucker

Canada and it costs the people in eastern Canada money to have goods taken to them from the west. In other words, it operates as a tariff does, and our party should give consideration, 1 submit, to the elimination of that brake upon the development of the country. That would be much better than increasing freight rates.
In regard to cooperatives, we know some are doing business in various parts of Canada. Our party in Saskatchewan has suggested that the federal government enact a dominion cooperative act as a necessary step in the complete functioning of the cooperative movement in Canada, as it is being carried on throughout the country. There should be provision for them to get incorporation from the dominion parliament.
As to the Hudson Bay railway, the western provinces set up a technical committee to study this problem and they recommend that, to give this route a fair trial, at least 16.000,000 bushels should be exported through that port this year. If 16,000,000 bushels were exported through that port it would eliminate all the deficits on the Hudson Bay railway; it would eliminate all deficits on the terminals, and it would give a real test to that port. Incidentally, it would save a great deal of extra money to the wheat growers of the country through the saving of over four cents a bushel freight on wheat exported through the port.
I urge the government, with all the emphasis I can exert, to bring pressure to bear upon the wheat board and everyone else involved to see to it that that great port, built, after all, with the money realized from the sale of western lands, shall be given the trial which it deserves and which we in the west believe will demonstrate that it is a workable means of communication not only between ourselves and Europe but between us and the maritime provinces of Canada. I would urge that upon the government.
I am aware that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in his trip overseas a year ago explored means whereby the Scotish cooperatives might take over some of our merchant ships to start trading out of and into Hudson bay. What they feel it possible to do in that regard I do not know, but I hope that everything will be done that can be done in developing that route.
In regard to floor prices, we have, as hon. members know, an Agricultural Prices Support Act. That is designed to put a floor price under farm products to ensure to the farmer an adequate and stable price for his products and to give him a return which will bear a fair relationship to that enjoyed by other

members of the community. We of the Saskatchewan Liberal party say that that should be adopted not only for the transition period from war to peace. We suggest that there should be a floor under farm prices as a permanent part of the economic set-up. There should be stability in the income of the farmer, who has to raise, care for and educate his family just as other people have to. He is as much entitled to stability in income as any other part of society, and we ask that consideration be given to making the Agricultural Prices Support Act a permanent part of the economic set-up.
In regard to income tax, everyone knows how hardly in recent years it has borne on the various parts of the country. Everyone knows it has had the effect of discouraging initiative and has made different people say that they do not want to work such long hours, while others say that they do not care to produce because they are afraid of the effect which the income tax might have on their net income. They think their efforts might not be worthwhile. The same is true throughout our whole economy. The farmer however has felt that the income tax act is one that has borne extraordinarily upon him.
I would point out two ways in which it has done so. Unfortunately there is a tendency on the part of some people, not farmers, to say that the farmer is taking an unreasonable attitude in this matter, but here are two ways in which he feels that the income tax has been unfair to him, and in these respects he would like to see a change made. In the first place, the family on a farm, the wife and children, make a real contribution to the income of the farmer, and yet that is not taken into consideration properly when he makes up his income tax returns. At the end of, say, ten years his financial standing is compared with that of what it was ten years previously and he is considered to have made all the money himself during that time. The farmer is certainly entitled to say that in the making of this money there were others who helped. Several people may help him to make the money because, while he may not pay it out at once to his children when they help him around the farm, he has in mind ultimately paying them by assisting them when they start on a farm of their own. Something definite should be done to take that situation into account and correct it.
The other point is this. In Saskatchewan we had sometimes as many as eight or nine years of crop failure. Men had worked for ten and fifteen years building up an estate for themselves and then had a succession of crop failures. Then they began to go into debt.

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
They put mortgages on their farms and sometimes lost everything they had made during a period of ten or fifteen years. Then with better crops they began to make money again and they want to pay off these mortgages and get into the same position they were in ten or fifteen years ago. But the income tax department says to them, as it does to other people in other lines of work, "We are not concerned about what you lost ten years ago; we are concerned only with what you are making today."
I give the government credit for being willing to average farm income over three years but I still say that something further should be done to take care of that particular situation of the man in western Canada who lost sometimes as many as nine or ten crops.
These are only some of the items that I wished to put before the house in the time at my disposal. I am sorry I could not cover all that I should like to have touched upon, but I thank the house for the indulgence it has shown me.

I am sure the house now regrets that it did not allow the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) to make from the very beginning the kind of speech he ended up with. I hope he will not take it amiss when I congratulate him on the excellent speech he has made in support of the programme which the C.C.F. has been advocating in Saskatchewan for so many years.
The debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne has done at least one thing. It has demonstrated that the war is over and that we are now face to face with all these problems which we failed to solve in the period between the two wars. The debate has also brought into clear focus the difference in policies as between the parties in this house dealing with our social and economic affairs. From observing the government's administration of affairs, and from listening to the speeches by the official opposition, it must be clear to anyone that there is no fundamental disagreement between them in the matter of policy. The chief difference that I see between the policies of the government and those of the official opposition is that the government wants to make an orderly retreat to the pre-war economy and the official opposition wants to make a disorderly retreat to the same ground. Neither party, it appears, has learned anything from the lessons of the twenty years of uneasy peace between the two wars nor, does it seem, have they learned anything from what happened during the six years of war itself, and a great deal happened during those years.
The other party, the Social Credit party, as far as I have been able to observe, believes in nearly all the fallacies and misconceptions on which the policies of the Liberals and Conservatives are based, and it has quite a number of its own fallacies besides. I do not think I am doing the Social Credit party any injustice when I say that it holds to the theory-this is good, orthodox, old-fashioned Liberal theory and I understand my hon. friends over to the right have adopted it-that the welfare of all is best served when each is concerned only with enhancing his own welfare. This philosophy is usually referred to as private enterprise, and my hon. friends have put themselves on record a dozen times during the present session that they are in favour of it. But to be completely fair with the Social Credit party, I must say that, although it adheres to the principle of capitalism-that is, private enterprise-as the best way of life, it also believes that there is a means by which we can avoid and overcome the evils associated with private ownership, namely, by the issue of a liberal supply of greenbacks.
"Liberal" is not the word; suitable and adequate.

Imagine that, to be suitable and adequate, it would have to be liberal; and I am afraid that the more liberal it would be, the more inadequate it would be. The Social Credit party not only believes that one can have his cake and eat it too, but also believes that one can eat the other fellow's cake and that he can still have it. That is the fundamental basis of their policy.
Nonsense.

For the first time during the session I agree with the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), that it is nonsense. The C.C.F. believes that the people should own, control and operate the means by which they must live. Not only that; we say that the masses of the people who do not own, control and operate the means by which they live, are not free.
Farms, too. Put them in also.
Yes; and I put a donkey in the barn.
You are afraid of that one.
Order.

Any people who do not own the means by which they live must go hat in hand to the people who do own those things
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

and ask for the right to live or the right to work in order that they may live. I should like to point out now that the policy we believe in, that of social ownership of the means of life, is becoming increasingly accepted throughout the world, so that today any man capable of reasoning who will look at the present world situation can come to only one conclusion, and that is that it is no longer a question of capitalism versus collectivism; it is a question today of what kind of collectivism the world is going to have. Shall it be totalitarian or democratic collectivism? The group with which I am associated believe in democratic collectivism; in other words, democratic socialism.
I wish to take a little time, Mr. Speaker, to deal with the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). I shall also, if I have time, deal with the Social Credit philosophy on which the amendment is based. Before dealing specifically with the subamendment, I wish to refer briefly to certain statements made by the leader of the Social Credit party when he spoke in this debate on February 3. At page 75 of Hansard, he is reported as saying:
Furthermore, I say to you, sir, that it is my belief and the belief of those in this group in the house, that any time the government sets out to achieve as its major conscious objective full employment, social security, or a planned economy, that government is going straight down the road to slavery of the people in the country.
I quoted that short paragraph because I wish to compare it with some other quotations from the hon. gentleman's speech. On page 76 of Hansard, just half a column distant from the quotation which I have just read, I find this:
I was very much disappointed that the speech from the throne made no mention of the government's intention to enter upon a bold, progressive and systematic programme of development in the north, and its colonization as well.
Put the passage I have just read along with the passage that I read first, and this is what you will find. The hon. member for Peace River told the house that any government that set out to achieve as its major conscious objective, full employment, social security or a planned economy, was leading the people down the path of slavery. The next moment he is criticizing the government for not planning in order to improve the standard of living of the people of this country.
Two entirely different things.

The only difference is that they were said at different times. I

imagine that any government that was going to enter on a bold, progressive and systematic programme would have to plan that programme. However, perhaps I am wrong.
I should like to quote another sentence from the same speech, on the same page of Hansard. I quote a sentence only, but it is long enough and there is enough in it to prove the point I desire to make. That point is that no matter what the Social Credit party says, or for what purpose it says it, that party believes in planning. This is the quotation:
Among their concrete achievements the Alberta government has recently commenced a vast scheme of clearing and colonization of lands in the Peace River country which in five years' time will result in 200,000 acres of new farms being brought under cultivation and production.
There again you have the hon. member for Peace River, who was criticizing the C.C.F. for advocating planning, who was telling the house that any government engaged in planning was taking the people down the path of slavery, congratulating the government of Alberta upon having done a little planning, a five-year plan if you like, in northern Alberta. So now what can we say of either the sincerity or the integrity of a party leader who condemns government planning when it is advocated by one party, who criticizes another party for not doing it, but who praises his own party for having done it? The C.C.F. believe that in our complex society production and distribution must be planned. What is more, we know it will be planned, for not to plan would be anarchy. The only question to be decided, then, is, will it be planned for the benefit of the country as a whole by the democratically elected representatives of the people, or will it be planned by a few individuals for their own profit? That is the situation confronting us today; those are the alternatives. Plan we must, and we must also accept the economic and social consequences of the kind of planning we do.
I now come to the Social Credit amendment, which would delete the Progressive Conservative amendment of no confidence and substitute four proposals. I am going to read only one of those four, and I shall state my purpose in reading it. The first proposal asks for the return to parliament of complete and effective control of Canada's financial policy. I am under the impression that this parliament now has and always has had full and complete control of Canada's financial policy. Of course it is open to question whether parliament has always exercised the power to make and control a financial policy in the interests of Canada. It is quite likely it has allowed other people to make the policy; but there is no doubt where the power to make such policies

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
lies. In that connection, however, the first prerequisite to the complete and effective control of a financial policy is complete and effective control of the financial institutions through which financial policies are carried out. In the opinion of this party, that implies the public ownership of our financial institutions; for instance, the public ownership of the chartered banks. The Social Credit party, however, is opposed to the public ownership of banks. They believe our financial institutions, along with all the other means of production, distribution and exchange, should be operated for private gain. This is a beautiful example of the contradiction between what the Social Credit party believes in and the results the Social Credit party wants to achieve.
I shall try to put the point briefly and, I hope, correctly. First, they say our financial institutions should be privately owned and, I believe it logically follows, operated for the private profit of the owners. Second, they want them operated for the social benefit of the community as well. I do not believe you can get those two things under those conditions. They fail to see, as so many other hon. members fail to see, that most of the time of this house is taken up in trying to harmonize the welfare of the community with the demands of an economic system that has for its purpose the exploitation of the community.
