Mr. Speaker, when the house rose for the dinner recess I was about to read section B of the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River. This is the section of the subamendment which contains the meat, if I may apply that term to a fallacy, of the social credit economic philosophy. It reads:
B. The use of the national credit to meet at least some of the financial requirements for essential services; and, as a guarantee that this country shall not again be subjected to financial depression, to make available to each and all Canadian citizens a proper portion of purchasing power which shall not first pass through the usual channels of industry, this on a basis calculated to maintain a balance between effective purchasing power in the hands of consumers and the aggregate of the prices of goods available for saje.
As I said, that is the meat of the social credit programme, the issuing of what they call debt-free money, with the suggestion or the assertion that it will neither add to prices
nor diminish the amount of income that any section of the community may receive. I claim that cannot be done.
I want you to note the phrase, "as a guarantee that this country shall not again be subjected to financial depression." The assumption of that phrase, an absolutely erroneous assumption, is that our depressions are financial. I wish to make the assertion, which I do not believe can be contradicted, that we have never had a financial depression in this country. The financial resources of the country, that is the currency and credit of the country, have always been adequate to distribute the goods and services produced. That is not to say that the goods and services produced have always been distributed to the people who needed them. They have not. But when that was not the case there was always sufficient money to do it. People may be in want wfiien there is a shortage of the things they need because under the capitalist system, which the social crediters support, goods are not produced to fulfil needs; they are produced to make a profit for the owners of the capital employed in producing them. That is the so-called private enterprise to which my hon. friends referred. If they serve the needs of the country, that is incidental. That is not the primary purpose of capitalist production.
The proof of that assertion lies in the fact that if you want anyone to invest in a project or undertaking the question you will be asked is, not what social good will accrue from it, but what profit will it make? If it will not make a profit you will not find investors for it. As long as it makes a profit, it will keep going; when it does not make a profit, the government has to take it over if it is an industry essential to the life of the community.
Prosperity and the amount of money in circulation are not necessarily dependent upon one another. The total amount of money and bank credit in circulation in Canada in 1938 was almost double that in circulation in 1929; yet 1929 was the peak, year of our prosperity and 1938 was a year of relative depression. I have the figures and I shall give them. The total money in circulation and the total bank deposits for 1929 were $2,934 million, while in 1938. as I said a year of relative depression when unemployment was five or six times what it was in 1929. the amount of money in circulation was $4,865 million, or nearly twice as much. Yet we are told that depressions are caused through our not having enough money.
At the present time everyone is predicting a depression, but our bank deposits and the
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

money in circulation are increasing all the time. Just before coming into the chamber I made a note of the savings deposits in our banks on January 31, 1946, and on January 31, 1947, and I found that in the period of one year .the savings deposits in the chartered banks of Canada had increased by approximately $570 million. Yet, as I said, everyone is predicting a depression.
I should like to read a short paragraph from a book that came into my hands only yesterday entitled "A Tax Programme for a Solvent America", by the committee on post-war tax policy. This is as recent as February, 1947, and in regard to money it says: Incidentally it should be noted that there is nowhere a lack of money. Even the stricken countries of Europe and the Orient have plenty of purchasing power, as the term goes. We have been provided with an impressive demonstration of the comparative sterility of money, as such. The great famine has demonstrated that people can starve, regardless of the quantity of money in circulation. Money is worthless in exchange unless there are goods to be exchanged. Whether it be paper money in Hungary, or bank deposits in Japan, the mere existence of purchasing power will not create bread and shoes.
Then they go on to say that what is required today is not money, but goods and the means to produce goods. After we have acquired those, the next thing to do is to provide a means of distributing those goods and services to the people who need them. Then we shall not need to worry about depressions, financial or otherwise.
Where will you get the money?
We have the money here, but the people who need the money do not have it and the people who have it, cannot use it.
Then you want more taxation.

There is no other way in which it can be done except by taxation, to take from those who have to give to those who have not, of course, unless we increase our total production. You cannot increase your .total production, as long as you are operating under the profit motive, because production is continually being restricted in order to increase prices. Read your cartels report.
And then we had overproduction in 1939.
That is what somebody told you. I never told you that.
There were plenty of goods then.

Yes, there were plenty of goods; that is what I am saying, but under the system which you support the people who produced those goods and needed them could not get them. That is what is wrong.
Let me give the house an idea of the amount of money that is available in savings deposits in our chartered banks. As of October 31, 1946, there were savings deposits in our chartered banks to an amount of over $3,476,000,000. The number of separate deposit accounts was 6,063,457, which works out at approximately one account for every two people in Canada. But when you come to classify these accounts you find that a great many people had very little money on deposit and that a very few people had a great deal. Of the 6,063,457 accounts, 5,290,728 were deposits of $1,000 or less, or an average deposit of $170. But when you come down to deposits in excess of $100,000, there were 971 accounts with an average deposit of $376,633.
Those who believe that they can remedy the situation by creating money are just deceiving simple people. I would say again that the struggle for survival in Britain today is another proof of the fact that it is not a scarcity of money that is the trouble. Monetary reform, of course, is an essential part of any programme designed to expand production for a higher standard of living, but as long as you leave the ownership, control and the direction and purpose of industry in private hands you will not accomplish much. For this reason alone, and there are plenty of others, this group cannot support the subamendment.
The hon. member for Peace River, speaking in the house the other night, made the statement that there was a feeling abroad that the Social Crediters had forsaken their monetary reform policy. Their amendment is sufficient proof that that is not the case, and I need not say anything more about it. But although they claim that they have not forsaken their monetary reform policy, I do claim that they have forsaken the basis on which William Aberhart's brand of social credit in Alberta was built up. Mr. Aberhart built up social credit in Alberta, not by extolling the virtues of free enterprise and big business, but by doing just the very opposite namely, attacking big business. I have in my hand a booklet with which my social credit friends, no doubt, used to be quite familiar but with which they have not been so familiar lately. It is the "Social Credit Manual," with the subtitle, "Social Credit as applied to the province of Alberta", written by William Aberhart, B.A., and with the further subtitle, "Puzzling questions and their answers"; and let me say that the answers are just as puzzling as the questions. In

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
stating the basic premise of social credit, this is what Mr. Aberhart says on page 5 of the manual:
It is the duty of the state through its government to organize its economic structure in such a way that no bona fide citizen, man, woman, or child, shall be allowed to suffer for lack of the bare necessities of food, clothing, and shelter, in the midst of plenty or abundance.
But listen to what the leader of the Social Credit party in this house said, speaking in this debate on February 3 last, as reported at page 75 of Hansard:
Furthermore, I say to you, sir, that it is my belief and the belief of those in this group in the house, that any time the government sets out to achieve as its major conscious objective full employment, social security, or a planned economy, that government is going straight down the road to slavery of the people in the country.
There is no contradiction there.

Mr. Aberhart said that it was the duty of the state to see that the people were provided for, but the hon. member for Peace River says that any government which attempts that is taking the people of the country down the road to slavery.
That is not right.

I have read the actual words and I think I understand English. There is a peculiar phrase used by the hon. member for Peace River to which I would draw attention. He said that any time the government sets out to achieve "as its major conscious objective" full employment, social security and so on. I imagine that if a government only made that a minor unconscious objective it would not be too bad. My social credit friends accuse the present government of socialistic or national planning, but let me tell them that if the government is doing anything of that kind it is of a minor nature and is done absolutely unconsciously.
Not a bad job at that.

My time is nearly up, but I wish to quote just a few more phrases from this little manual on social credit. If social credit were possible it would involve so much control that any control which might take place under the planned economy advocated by this group would be absolute freedom in comparison. The Social Crediters are to have no taxes but they are to have a levy. William Aberhart said in this manual:
Thus the province will be able to collect a levy that will provide the basic dividends to distribute to the various citizens.
The citizens were to get dividends, and then they would pay for them, of course, by a levy, not a tax. Mr. Aberhart goes on to say:
To illustrate this let us take a bushel of wheat say at a just price of sixty cents. Fifty-five cents of this is to go to the farmer and will provide a fair commission on his turnover. Five cents will be set aside for the government levy. The wheat is sold to the miller who grinds it into flour. The cost of grinding will be covered by the shorts and bran and other by-products of the process. This will produce about forty pounds of flour. We will suppose that the flour sells for $1.10, ten cents of which is again given to the government as its levy. The flour is next turned to the baker who makes it into bread which he sells at seven cents a loaf. The forty pounds of flour with the water and other ingredients would make fifty loaves of bread. Suppose the government levy on this bread was a cent a loaf. That would give an additional fifty cents levy. Thus from a bushel of wheat, processing it to flour, the government would be able to collect possibly sixty-five cents.
The original price of the bushel of wheat was only sixty cents! And they tell you that there would be no taxes under social credit. They may say that they have changed their policy and that things would be different, but in reply to one of the questions asked in this little manual, "How long would it take to put social credit into effect in Alberta?" the answer is, "Eighteen months." Well, Mr. Speaker, they have been in power in Alberta for twelve years now and any idea of putting social credit into effect has absolutely disappeared. Indeed, they are so far away from social credit now that the people who were once afraid of the Social Credit government are now the people who are financing it.

Mr. Speaker. I shall not trespass very long on the time of the house tonight, and I was not minded to take part in this debate had it not been for the fact that I must always be conscious of the housing conditions in my own riding of Rosedale, which is very much in the centre of the city of Toronto, a little bit to the east toward the river Don. This morning I received the report of the building commissioner of our city, Mr. Iv. S. Gillies, which gives the total amount spent on construction during 1946 and divides it into the various classes. Before giving the house the figures which the commissioner has outlined, may I say that I am amazed at the complacency of the Canadian people in regard to housing. I was also amazed at the complacency of our people during the depression years and at the way in which they stood the hard times they were up against and their inability to find work during the period when the Liberal government was in power, even though they
The Address-Mr. Jackman

were able and willing to work. May I recall to you, sir, that at that time the chief occupations of many of those who were unable to find work were bricklaying, plastering, carpentering and other house-building activities. There was just no substantial housing, if any at all, being carried on in Toronto at that time.
When I visit some of the people in the areas where housing conditions are bad, see the overcrowding and the number of families living in a single dwelling unit I cannot help avoid feeling that the Indians in Central America and in other countries are better housed than are some of our own people.
Last year I mentioned that I had visited one large old house which had no fewer than fifty-three people living in it. This house had practically no facilities in it. As I remember it, there was one bath with a cold-water tap, and that was all. What has happened to that place? It has been tom down to make room for a moving-picture house. I inquired where the people were. For the most part they have been moved to Stanley barracks which, as many hon. members will know, is a very old stone barracks near the Toronto exhibition. I recall that some thirty or thirty-five years ago it was so old that it was being used as a prison centre for Austrian prisoners of war. Yet that is where we are quartering our own Canadian people.
May I recall here, as my colleague, the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) did recently, the words of Brigadier Douglas H. Storms, building manager of housing enterprises, dated October 10. He said:
Plant extensions, theatres, garages, stores, summer cottages, dance halls and hot-dog stands are under construction. At the same time people are living in the worst distress for lack of housing. On one street of small houses in New Toronto-
That is in one of our newer districts.
-we found each house was occupied on the average by nineteen people.
Last November I made an inquiry of the emergency housing centre where people file their appeals for some kind of shelter, and I found that there were 7.300 unfilled applications for any kind of shelter whatsoever. It was reported to me then that that very night an R.C.A.F. veteran of sixteen months' overseas service, his wife, his daughter of thirteen and his boy of twelve had been picked up in a public park because they had no place to go, and were endeavouring to stay there for the

night. Apparently the man had been staying at a hotel but a veteran's gratuity does not last long at hotel rates.
I would feel that I was trespassing on the time of the house in pointing out the need for housing, but if all hon. members could be taken in the congested areas of some of our larger cities and see the picture as it actually is I am convinced that something more would be done than has been attempted by this government. In 1944-I put this on the record merely to refresh the memories of hon. members-the advisory committee on housing estimated Canada's shortage of housing units at 600,000. At least 300.000 families are doubled up; but what cares this government as long as it can let sleeping dogs lie? What amazes me is the complacency of our people. Why they stand for it when they see so much building of other kinds going on all about them, I do not know. Did the Curtis report not show that there are over 300.000 substandard dwellings? According to the figures of the minister, 60.000 housing units were constructed last year, or not much more than enough to take care of the annual growth plus the wastage, because even houses, particularly temporary ones, wear out in time.
Judged by its actions and its lack of planning, there is good ground for believing that the government does not take the housing shortage seriously. Certainly it does not consider that there is any real emergency but just a comfortable shortage of houses which can be made up when employment is not so plentiful as it is today. Is it possible that the government believes that because the population of Canada is little if any greater than it was in the pre-war years, and since there are certainty no fewer housing units than there were before the war, conditions cannot be very bad? These are true facts which may seem to give rise to the specious conclusion that there is no dire distress as far as housing is concerned. Our population has not grown and we have not had houses bombed, so where is the housing shortage? What the people will put up with, if one would investigate the actual conditions in our city in the way of unhealthy housing conditions, is something which staggers the imagination. Is the government even conscious of the problem? If so, its pain must be so great that it has taken a sleeping potion to lull itself into self-satisfaction and utter complacency.
Let me now come to the figures in the annual report of the building commissioner,

The Address-Mr. Jackman
Mr. K. S. Gillies of the city of Toronto. He says in his little foreword:
Commercial and industrial building formed the larger portion of the year's work while housing took second place.
That was a masterpiece of understatement. The facts as shown in the booklet are as follows:	In 1946-these are actual construction
-the total value of all buildings erected was $22,232,000, while the total value of housing units, including apartments, was $3,291,000. In other words, fifteen per cent of all the money spent on construction in the city of Toronto in 1946 was devoted to housing units and the other eighty-five per cent to a variety of construction projects which had nothing whatsoever to do with housing our people or looking after our veterans who had been away from Canada for five or six years while other people may have been getting a roof over their heads, but who had nothing to go to when they came back. During the year there were 843 permits issued for housing out of a total of 11,242 permits for building and alterations of one sort and another. Therefore we may see what we have to look forward to in 1947. Out of 11,242 permits, 843 permits were issued for housing. What other construction was there in the city of Toronto last year? Commercial and industrial buildings amounted to $17,090,000, or 77 per cent; schools and churches, $399,000, or 1-5 per cent and, miscellaneous, $1,511,000, or 6-5 per cent. With a score of fifteen per cent for housing, that category certainly came a very poor second to commercial and industrial buildings, with seventy-seven per cent of the total amount of money going into that class. May I point out that in the construction of four movie theatres, two garages and three warehouses, taking a total of $2,181,000, that amount for this very small number of units of large commercial projects took up as much as two-thirds of the total that went into housing units in Toronto. The number of new housing units was only 636. probably sufficient to house about 2,400 people; but the number of applications for emergency shelter of any kind was, as I have mentioned, at the first of November, 7,300, and this may be compared with 636 housing units constructed last year.
How are we facing the problem? We are not even nibbling at it at the present time. Is the fifteen per cent for residential construction out of the total building construction in Toronto to be considered normal? After the last war, in 1922, which is as far as the figures in the little book I had at my disposal went, the percentage of housing construction to total construction in the city was
62 per cent. Last year it was la per cent. For several years following 1922 the percentage hovered around 60 per cent. In 192829 it was 30 per cent and from there it continued around 40 per cent until 1939 when it dropped to 28 per cent. Since then, the percentages of residential construction to total construction have been 40, 26, 38, 35, 23 per cent, and in 1947, under the present iniquitous system, 15 per cent, an all-time record low.
The dollar value is pretty much the same. In 1922 and following, residential construction was $22 million; in 1946 it was $3,291,000, or about one-seventh last year of what it was in 1922, as far as housing units were concerned.
The government may well wonder why any member or party who is for freeing business and production from their chains, and who is against controls in general, would advocate building controls. In the first place, the housing situation in Canada, particularly in city ridings such as my owTn, was never good. This government did nothing about building houses in the depression years. No houses could be built in the war years, for good reasons, and there has been an influx of population. The demand for housing so far exceeds supply that rental controls and, perhaps even more so, building controls are necessary. The result of no building control has already been shown. Commercial enterprises have plenty of money and the cost of building is therefore but a small item in their budget. They are not very much concerned with how much they pay for building. The ordinary citizen, however, and particularly the veteran, is very much concerned, because his pocketbook is limited and housing is one of the main expenses in his budget.
Even under proper government supervision the acuteness of the housing shortage cannot be relieved overnight. At the present rate of progress it will take many years to overcome it. and until it is overcome I presume we shall be under the necessity of rental control, which has many bad features as well as some good ones. The Liberal government has refused to accept responsibility for priorities. It has told the municipalities that they can put on their 'own building restrictions. This was entirely unsatisfactory and is entirely unsatisfactory today, because the problem has always been a national one. The reason for that is that if an industry wanted to expand or a new movie was to be set up, it would go to that place or that city where there were no restrictions, and no municipality was willing -and again this is the effect of politics; it is quite natural-to lose the chance of having a new industry established within the confines
The Address-Mr. Jackman

of its own borders, so it took down the bars and allowed any commercial or industrial project to go ahead.
The question of priorities is one which, if it is to be effective at all, must be exercised from Ottawa where a balance can be maintained betwen various competing muncipali-ties for industrial projects which are vital and necessary in some cases and for housing which we know is extremely urgent. The Liberal government refuses to be responsible for the welfare of the people and to control the type of buildings to be erected. It is left to the men or the businesses who can pay the most. As Mayor Robert Saunders of Toronto said:
Our city fathers tried desperately to have the federal government maintain a strict control over all building and see that the many materials in short supply were directed first to home building. It was a problem that only the federal government have the power to control and direct.
Last evening we were given the lumberman's point of view on timber controls when my colleague the hon. member for Victoria, Ontario, (Mr. Hodgson) spoke. If we accept the suggestion that forty per cent of Canada's increased timber cut should be allowed for export-and I use that figure of forty per cent as a rough one because I understand that on the west coats two-thirds of the volume of lumber may be exported and in the central provinces only one-third, and here I may remark it is no wonder that the western lumber people feel that controls are not too unsatisfactory when they can export two-thirds of the output at the rather attractive prices which they get in the export market- if, I repeat, we say that forty per cent of our lumber is to be exported in order to maintain our trade channels and be fair to other countries, so that sixty per cent is left for domestic allocation, then we must make sure that the sixty per cent is fairly allocated among those who are entitled to lumber for building purposes.
If it is left to the present system those who have the longest purse-and that is certainly not the ordinary prospective home owner- are the ones who are to get the lion's share of this lumber. If we had a system of priorities from Ottawa it would mean that sixty per cent would be available to those who had a priority for housing, and for veterans housing in particular. Then, if there were no price controls and more lumber were brought to the domestic market, sixty per cent or greater, we would find that too large a percentage of it or too great an amount would not be used in building, because the amount of lumber

consumed must be limited by the capacity of the building industry and the number of trained building workers.
Furthermore, I do not think that if controls were taken off lumber-not export control but price control-we would find that lumber would go up much in price. The minister suggested that if it went sky-high-I do not know what figure he had in mind, but no doubt a substantial amount-it might add $200 or $300 to each house. Already builders have found price resistance developing in respect of smaller houses which are being built at the present time. The people do have some respect for the purchasing power of the dollar; if they do not get good value they will refuse to invest, and it xyill be found that, instead of its being a seller's market, it will become a buyer's market. At least the scales would be held in balance. So long as we have controls, the controllers will find reasons for continuing their own existence. It is only natural that they should think that way.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, that even now if moving picture theatres, dance halls, hotels and bowling alleys were eliminated, the shortage in lumber and many other building supplies and also of labour would be pretty well done away with as far as sufficient to put on a real house-building programme is concerned. The only effect of lumber controls is that the short purse of the veteran and the prospective home builder cannot acquire very much lumber, but the long purses of these moving picture magnates and those who are putting up the other forms of commercial or industrial enterprises get the lumber and get it at a cheap price. Certainly the lumber is not going to the builder of homes. I mention those four classes, moving-picture theatres, dance halls, hotels and bowling alleys, because they are commercial undertakings and not because of any lofty sentiments. I believe that none of those forms of commercial activity creates jobs for any great number of our people. One cannot make the excuse that, by allowing dance halls and moving-picture theatres to be erected, we are providing places where employment will be given to a substantial number of our people in less prosperous times.
May I mention here that I do not know how weighty the consideration is which the minister gave to this vexed problem of bousing, which certainly is not being met in the riding of Rosedale. But on February 7, when he announced a new plan for rental housing, whereby if a man built houses for rent and gave priority to the veteran he would be allowed double depreciation, I asked the minister just how much the

The Address-Mr. Jackman
depreciation was now, so that I could form some estimate of what the double depreciation would be. His words were, "I have not the figures at my fingertips, but my impression is that the present rate is four per cent; if so, the new rate will be eight per cent." I began to figure out just what this might mean to the housing industry and whether or not new rental houses might be constructed. When I checked the figures in Hansard the next day, I found that the four per cent had become two and a half per cent, and double that is five per cent. I am not complaining about the minister's memory, but I feel that when a major policy is announced in this house, some thought should be given to it by the minister, because the difference between being able to write off five per cent over the next few years as against being able to write off eight per cent, is substantial. Of course the five per cent does go for the whole life of the building, until the whole investment is written off.
But the point I am making is this. Everyone feels that if you put up a house today for rental, you are probably putting it up at inflated values; and you are a little bit concerned that, if you have to get rid of it over the next five or ten years, you cannot get your money back. However, if the minister had put forward a real programme of depreciation-not of five per cent but double four per cent, or eight per cent, let us say-it would be found that over the next five or eight years the man who might put up that house for rental would be able to write off enough of his depreciation that he would not have to worry about getting out of it whatever value he still had left in it; whereas at the present time he has to carry it perhaps for ten years or longer, before he may be able to get his money back, because he may have to sell in a market which is not as buoyant as the present one.
I believe that if the government will take the controls off building supplies and put the control on permits for the class of building undertaking which is most needed from the social point of view, and most needed by our veterans, the housing shortage in this country would be ended much more quickly than it will be under the present system.

May I ask my hon. friend
one question? Will he tell us where in the city of Toronto residential property can be bought in acreage sufficient to put up, say, 1,000 houses?

I am glad the minister asked that question, because I had meant to cover it. I was a little concerned, after I got
the report from the building commissioner, about where all the building was to be done in the city of Toronto, because the report itself confined itself to the actual geographical limits of the city. Within 150 yards of where I happen to live there are two very large spaces where apartment houses could be built. I have consulted with at least half a dozen of my colleagues, and while I do not know where one could put up 1,000 houses as a unit in Toronto, or even 250 houses, nevertheless there are a number of spaces where houses can be put up, particularly apartment houses.
I think the real answer to the question is this. Where these warehouses and moving-picture theatres are being put up one could no doubt put up apartment houses. But more strongly, I think, the answer to my main charge of misdirection of building materials and building labour is the fact that on the outskirts of the city there is considerable housing activity, in the construction of workmen's houses particularly. I am interested in some of them myself. I know the struggle which the manager of the company I am interested in is forced to carry on in order to get bricks, lumber, foremen, boss carpenters and whatnot. The only reason that we are able to put up houses at all is that the company is able to buy and pay cash for materials in the winter time when some other builders are not able to acquire them. We have done a reasonably good job, but it is a struggle all the time. The reason that materials and labour cannot be obtained is that so much goes into buildings which, I shall not say are non-essential, but which, to my mind, have less social priority than housing in the city of Toronto. That is the reason why we are not getting on with the house-building programme as fast as we otherwise might. If anyone takes on a project of 100 houses on the outskirts of Toronto, he will find that it is a tooth-and-nail job-nail in the literal sense as well as the metaphorical one-to get any progress at all. Only the most skilful manager is able to erect houses, because of the misdirection and the lack of control on the part of the federal government.

I have one more question and this is the last. Am I right in saying that my hon. friend, in giving his statistics for the city of Toronto, left out all the house-building in the surrounding areas to which he is now referring?
I just said that the book I have is confined to the geographical area of Toronto.

Exactly.
The Address-Mr. Shaw

I forget the total figure for the Dominion of Canada, which is not too pleasant anyway, although it is certainly better than fifteen per cent. I am concerned about my own riding and about conditions there, and I should like to take the minister there. The total for the Dominion of Canada, as given in answer to the question of my colleague the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Eleming) was $383 million of total construction last year, of which $200 million, or fifty-two per cent, was for housing units. But even that is not good enough. When I know the situation locally in my own town, I think I have the right to come here and ask the government to do more for the people, who, to my mind, are much too complacent.

Mr. Speaker, prior to 5.40 o'clock this afternoon it was my intention to speak for only twenty minutes and to adhere strictly to certain previously prepared notes. Thanks to the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), I shall be obliged to extend my time and to move away from that previously charted course. This afternoon and again this evening the hon. member for Vancouver East indulged in one of his usual pastimes, that of jerking from their context words, phrases, clauses and paragraphs, endeavouring to convey to this house a definitely erroneous impression. In so doing, he managed to work himself into the usual lather. Before the dinner recess, in referring to social credit he indulged in such expressions or partial expressions as "concerned only with personal welfare," and, as I say, endeavoured to create the impression that the members of this group were concerned only about their personal welfare.

I never said anything of the kind, that any member of this house or any member of any other party was concerned only with his personal welfare. I referred to it as a system; and I do not want to have any implications of that kind.

The hon. gentleman wasted his forty minutes this afternoon and evening; I hope he will permit me to utilize mine. I said the hon. gentleman sought to create an impression, and I stick to what I said. He referred to "an old-fashioned theory." Goodness knows what he had in the back of his mind! He referred to "a liberal supply of greenbacks." He must have been in the pond with the frogs. He made statements like these: "eat his cake and have it, too"; "eat the other fellow's cake, and still let him have it"- such utter nonsense!

I know it is nonsense, but
that is what you are advocating.

It was manufactured by the hon. gentleman himself, and the expression is certainly nonsense. Because certain hon. gentlemen opposite laughed at him-and certain hon. gentlemen opposite will laugh at almost anything-he waxed even more eloquent. He went on to ridicule the assertion, I presume of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), with respect to the effective control of monetary policy. He asserted in all his dignity that we at present exercise full and complete control of monetary policy; then he proceeded to talk about contradictions, and said the only possible way we could have effective control was to nationalize the Bank of Canada.
I did not say anything of the kind.
Or rather the chartered banks.
Do not misquote me and I will not interrupt you.
Mr. Speaker-
Every time you misquote you are going to be interrupted.
Mr. Speaker, will you please ask the hon. member to sit down and stay down?	.
Mr. Speaker, will yop tell the hon. gentleman not to misquote me, and I will not interrupt him.
The hon. gentleman used the words "financial institutions" and I take that to include the Bank of Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He said the chartered banks.
It includes more than the Bank of Canada.
Let us say it includes them all; it is still a contradiction.

Order. I would ask the hon. member who has the floor to address himself to the Chair.
Mr. SHAW': I apologize, Mr. Speaker; I thought I was doing so. I noticed that in speaking of nationalization the hon. gentleman did not proceed to give us the excellent illustration that could have been given by dealing with the British policy with respect to the nationalization of their bank. I noticed, too, he did not go out of his way to tell us why the Labour government of Australia and the Labour government of New Zealand have not nationalized their banks. Members of the C.C.F. party usually refer to those govern-

The Address-Mr. Shaw
ments as being counterparts of the C.C.F. party, but at times it is convenient to forget that expression. I noticed, too, that he did not go on and tell us about all the virtues of the Russian system of financial nationalization. There I believe he would find the only existing institution of the nature he describes and the virtues of which it would seem he extols. He also went on to indulge in the expression "'socialization of the means of life," but I noticed he did not go out of his way to enlarge upon that expression. I believe he realizes as well as I do that it includes agriculture, which is one of the basic means of life in this country. When he was asked by an hon. member in this group whether ft included the farms, he made some ridiculous comment about a donkey. Well, I do not think the hon. member for Vancouver East could even convince a donkey that nationalization is essential. Then the hon. gentleman went on to refer to democratic socialism. I say there is no such animal; and he has said, nothing in this house today or at any other time that would serve to convince me and my colleagues that there is. As he spoke this afternoon, an expression came to my mind, a statement which is credited to Lenin; for all I know these may be his exact words: "Social democracy is a politically preposterous term. Under socialism, democracy withers away," and I agree with Lenin in that statement.
You and Lenin!

The hon. member for Qu'-Appelle (Mrs. Strum) has interjected an observation which brings me to a question I should like to direct to the hon. member for Vancouver East. Does that peculiar type of democratic socialism go by another name, that of Marxian socialism?
No.
To the best of my knowledge that question has never been answered by my hon. friend.	_
It is answered now to my hon. friend's knowledge, if he has any. It does not.
I did not hear what the hon. gentleman said.
I said, "no".
Fine.

Nobody ever spoke better for Marx than the hon. member
does.

I am sure the hon. member will have some interesting words for the hon.
member for Skeena (Mr. Archibald), who not so long ago extolled the virtues of Karl Marx right on the floor of this house and, I would almost assume, in the name of his party.
I should now like to call certain witnesses in connection with the hon. gentleman's observations respecting social credit. I wish to direct my remarks and my quotations expressly to the backbenchers of the C.C.F. party, since probably some have not had their attention directed to the debates which took place in this house about 1935. I propose now to take them back to that period. I have before me Hansard of March 26, 1935. Those were the days when the skids were under the Bennett government. An election was in the offing. Many people, and especially politicians, may have had numerous nightmares about that time. I hope the hon. gentleman will not attribute these words to a nightmare, because if he was not under the influence of a nightmare at that time he must be under the influence of a nightmare today. At page 2138 of Hansard for that date I find an amendment moved by Mr. George Coote, who, I understand, is now a director of the Bank of Canada, and seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East. This is the amendment:
That the amendment be amended by striking out all the words after the word "Canada" and adding thereto the following: "and would appear to be based upon the assumption that poverty and debt are inevitable conditions within the country;
and whereas the real and potential wealth of the nation, based upon our natural resources and our capacity to produce, is such as to make-possible an abundant provision for all the requirements of our people;
Therefore, this house is of the opinion that the government should take immediate action to ensure the fullest and most equitable distribution possible of our socially-created wealth and that, as a first step in this direction, the measures which may be necessary to meet the pressing needs of the farmers and the unemployed should be financed by the social credit of Canada, thus avoiding a further increase in the debt burden of the country."
The present hon. member for Cariboo (Mr.. Irvine) spoke in support of that amendment to the budget of 1935. I call the hon. member for Cariboo as a witness against the hon. member for Vancouver East, and I should like to quote from page 2323 of Hansard, April 2, 1935, where the hon. member for Cariboo-I do not know what his constituency was then; he has changed quite a number of times-is reported as having said:
I submit at the outset that that remedy is one which will very soon have to be accepted not only by this government but by all governments in the world.
The Address-Mr. Shaw

He is referring to social credit.
I make that prediction because in my opinion there is only one alternative to that, and that is to witness the complete collapse of civilization itself.
Those are the application, of the social credit principles set out by the present hon. member for Cariboo. He went on to say:
We make this suggestion then to the government, and we solicit the support also of the opposition for a policy applied to the only problem in Canada, the problem of distributing the abundance which our natural resources, our skilled mechanics and our technical equipment make possible to our people.
In other words, the only problem is that of distribution.
This proposal assumes that there is enough and to spare of every commodity essential to life, to supply every person indefinitely; but that there is too little money in the hands of the consumers to permit the proper distribution of these essential commodities to be made.
I move on to page 2324, the same speaker:
So much, then, for the assumption that there is an abundance of supplies. As to the other assumption contained in our amendment, that there is too little money, I think the fact that there has been a shortage of money for purchasing power has been very adequately and emphatically demonstrated. I direct the attention of this house once more to the analyses and the mathematical demonstration of Major Hugh Douglas, of London, -who I think has shown more completely and more thoroughly than any other economist of his time the scarcity of money and the causes of that scarcity. But he is by no means the only one who has demonstrated that fact. Foster and Catching have demonstrated it in the United States; Kitson, Keynes, [Right Hon. Reginald McKenna and numerous others have proved beyond the shadow of a doubt to every intelligent student of the question that there is not sufficient money in circulation at a given time to buy the goods on the shelves at the prices at which those goods are marked, and that while that is so those goods cannot be distributed.
I have just one more short quotation I should like to make. I agree with what he said; I have no grievance with the hon. member for Cariboo.
Keep on; you are making a good speech.

I hope the hon. member can convince the hon. member for Vancouver East. I quote again from page 2325:
To make the situation worse machinery is becoming more and more automatic as the industrial process goes on, and the use of solar power, steam, oil, gas, electricity has not only made it possible to produce sufficient goods with a very much reduced number of workers, but has vastly increased production, in some instances far beyond the capacity of the people to consume even if they had the money to buy the goods, which they have not. Moreover the tendency is
[Mr. Shaw.l
towards further mechanical progress, which will still further reduce the number of Workers required and further increase output.
And then again:
Being unable to find markets at home through lack of purchasing power as I have described, the producers of all nations enter into keener competition for whatever foreign market there may be, thus the economic basis of war.
I should like to be able to read all the hon. member's speech because I think it was an excellent one. I think he delivered that speech only after the most careful study. I am sure that when he made the speech he was absolutely convinced, because I am satisfied that he would not have made it unless he were. I come now to the vote on that amendment. Here are the yeas:
Messrs. Coote, Gardiner, Garland (Bow River), Heaps, Irvine, Lucas, Maelnnis, Miss MaePhail, Mitchell-
I will refer to that in just a moment. Speakman, Spencer, Woodsworth.
The Gardiner mentioned is not the present Minister of Agriculture, but the Mitchell referred to is the present Minister of Labour. I say that he, by virtue of having supported that amendment, has declared along with the hon. member for Cariboo that this is the alternative to the collapse of civilization. I should like to go on quoting because I want to show the hon. member for Vancouver East that when it comes to going back into the archives and digging out dusty books we are ready to engage in such a contest with him at any time. I am sure that we shall be able to bring forward assertions and things which are more embarrassing to him than anything he can direct at us.
There is nothing embarrassing yet as far as I am concerned.
Was he having a nightmare, or is he having a political nightmare now?
Political jitters now.

Things of this kind remind me that in one of the states of the United States-I do not remember which one at the moment-a professor of pharmacy is working on what I think they call a system of odoriferous advertising, and with a considerable amount of success. After listening to the hon. member for Vancouver East tonight and a.fter watching the developments of their organization over the years, if we apply that newly determined practice of odoriferous advertising, then their programme or platform will smell to high heaven.
I should like to deal now with things more pleasant. During this debate, repeated reference has been made to our war veterans and

The Address-Mr. Shaw
their general rehabilitation. I listened with dismay the other day to the frank and honest admission by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) that things were not all right with all veterans houses. I think it was the honest thing for the minister to do to make that statement on the floor of this house, but I would submit that the defence which I have noticed already in the papers, namely, that there was a lack of suitable materials and competent workmen, does not stand up very well.
If we go outside the activities of certain of these contractors we shall find that, with the same materials and with the same so-called incompetent workmen, houses have been built which are a credit to the builders. I am thinking for the moment of the small holdings set up near the city of Red Deer. Those houses were constructed in an excellent fashion and they are a credit to those responsible for their erection and for the supervision. I say, therefore, that the contractors cannot take refuge in the assertions that they are now making.
. I regret that all the people of Canada-I believe that was the expression used by the Minister of Veterans Affairs-will have to pay the seven or eight hundred thousand dollars needed to put these houses in a state of repair. Possibly that cannot be avoided, but personally I wish to say that the taxpayers of this country are not going to look with any degree of happiness upon that prospect. As I have said, the houses on the small holdings at Red Deer were well constructed. Unless we are extremely careful I am fearful that those veterans will encounter difficulties in paying for these homes. Unless we establish guarantees essential to the economic welfare of these boys, they will find the handling of a $7,000 or $8,000 debt a colossal undertaking.
With respect to land settlement under the Veterans Land Act, at first there was a good deal of criticism with regard to the slowness of the inspections of land which these veterans had applied for, and there were a certain number of complaints with regard to the rejections. But I wish to pay a compliment to those persons in the soldier settlement board office in Red Deer. We live in an exceptionally fine part of Canada. It is one of the finest mixed farming areas between the two coasts, and consequently we have had a tremendous number of applications from exservice men for settlement in that area. Considering all handicaps I think the responsible officials have done an admirable job in handling their inspections and everything else relating to these applications.
We should have learned something from world war I, and I think we did. It is no kindness to put a man on a piece of land that is not agriculturally productive. We saw that happen all through my part of the country after the last war. I think it is wise to guard against a thing of that kind happening again, and generally speaking I believe they are guarding against it in that part of the country. On the other hand, however, unless we are prepared to do something to guarantee a stable price structure for agricultural products, I fear that the majority of these boys will lose their title to their properties after they have fully paid for them and that many of them will never be in a position to pay for them fully. These veterans can certainly be crushed under their debt load just as thousands of veterans were crushed under their debt load after world war 1. The realization of this fact impresses upon one more and more the importance of sections 1 and 2 of the social credit amendment to the amendment.
Finally, with respect to these veterans, may I say that I am pleased with the exceptionally good work done in most of these vocational schools across the countiy. We have one of them in Red Deer and it is functioning admirably. The results that are obtained from the type of instruction given there will never be fully known.
I have spoken favourably about those things of which I could speak favourably. I now have two criticisms to make and I hope they will prove to be constructive. The first has to do with veterans' education, and the second has to do with the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act.
We all know that students, following high school graduation, during the war enlisted in great numbers in the Canadian armed forces. Some of these boys spent five or six years in our armed services and, upon their return, many of them made application for university entrance. After months of delay, many of them were advised that they would have to take certain brush-up tests, and I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that they were not given an adequate opportunity of preparing properly for these tests. As a matter of fact, some of them had only two or three weeks in which to prepare to write tests for three days upon all they were presumed to have learned while attending school. That was not fair. A great many of them failed, or at least the results indicated that they would have to proceed to take a course in the veterans high school in the spring. Many of these lads are now in these veterans high schools, where a cramming, jam-
The Address-Mr. Shaw

ming process is going on which I say it is not fair to many of these ex-service men. You cannot expect them to absorb the great masses of material which they are asked to absorb in such a short period of time in order to qualify to enter our universities.
Moreover, our universities are demanding a higher standard from our ex-service personnel than they are demanding from civilians. 1 ask, why? I am not complaining if these veterans are forced to attain the same standard in their examinations as the non-veteran, but they are required to attain a higher standing to remain in the universities. That is the rankest type of discrimination. These boys have benefited in many ways through being in the armed services. They have travelled and associated with their fellow men, which in itself is one of the finest forms of education, and they go into these universities better qualified to take these courses than many civilian boys and girls who are just leaving high school and going into the universities.
Overseas the Canadian army educational services functioned. I do not want to be too critical, but I must draw this to the attention of the minister and ask for an explanation. Many of these boys left high school to go into the armed services, and many of them lacked one or two credits for university entrance. While overseas, they took through the Canadian army educational services what they believed to be qualifying courses to enter a university. Many of them came back as late as last summer and made application for university entrance and were told point-blank that the courses they had taken were not courses which qualified them for university entrance. I wonder how widespread that condition was. I have several personal cases I can bring to the minister's attention.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Has the hon. member addressed any of these questions to the department?

I shall not presume to answer that question offhand. I am usually in the habit of directing my problems to the appropriate ministers. Anyway we shall talk that over. I wonder if some of our universities were deliberately endeavouring to keep some of these boys out. I hope they will answer that question. Some of these boys wanted to take medical courses. They are now in veterans high schools and they are being told by the universities, "Why don't you take a B.A.?" A B.A. is, in my opinion, as useful as an O.B.E. when it comes to earning a living The universities should not be endeavouring 
to put pressure on these boys to take the B.A. course when the boys I think of particularly,
are anxious to take a medical course and will make good doctors, and surely Canada is in need of more doctors. I hope the minister will give this matter some consideration.
I should now like to turn to the Veterans Business and Professional Loans Act. I am glad the minister is here because this is another example of discrimination. I understand that this act was passed last year but did not become operative until this year; on January 15. someone suggests. Most of our boys came back before 1947. They were anxious to become reestablished and had to grab business opportunities as they came to their attention. Many of them went into business and put all their persona] capital into an enterprise. Some of them borrowed from the banks and other lending institutions on very short terms. Now these lads have come forward and made application to secure a loan under the act to spread what they have borrowed from the lending institution over a longer period of time. They have been told:	No, there is no provision
in the act for that purpose. One of the minister's officials-I do not believe in quoting from letters I have received-did indicate to me that, while certain amendments might be made to the act later on, there was.no possibility of the government looking upon such an amendment with favour. Personally I think he stepped just a little bit out of his proper sphere. After all, I think we should be the ones to determine that as a parliament of Canada, operating in conjunction with the government.
Let me just suggest one case, Mr. Speaker. Here are some lads who put $10,000 of their own money into a newspaper business. This business had functioned successfully for years and years. These boys had to step out and borrow $10,000, which has to be repaid in five years. Naturally that will prove extremely burdensome to them, but they cannot secure relief under this act. I say to the minister that unless there is some extremely good reason for not doing so, the act should be amended to make provision for such cases. The rate of interest w'ould likely not be any lower. The rate of interest under this act is, I believe, five per cent. They are paying the lending institutions five per cent. Let me go on record as asserting that that is altogether too high beause many veterans and non-veterans are borrowing from certain institutions and individuals at rates of interest considerably less than that and the govern-

The Address-Mr. Shaw
ment is also offering lower rates of interest on certain of its own transactions as a government.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that I should move on. I hate to be accused of having taken up my full time just because I am allowed forty minutes. I have enough notes here to go on for possibly four hours, and therefore I believe I would be justified in proceeding for the other seven or eight minutes. I wish to say a word or two about the amendment, not the amendment to the amendment but the amendment itself. We feel that our social credit amendment to the Conservative amendment is necessary in the light of the negative character of the Conservative amendment. We are offering no argument against the Progressive Conservatives' right to offer such an amendment, but I am convinced that a concise alternative to government policy should have been presented.
Since the amendment does not contain an alternative proposal, it must be assumed that I am being asked to vote want of confidence with the suggestion that if the house and the country have no confidence in the government, then they must have confidence in the Progressive Conservative party. I say that that is a wrong assumption. I am not going to vote in such a way as to put myself in a position of being accused of that because, in the light of their declared policy, I for one cannot accept the Progressive Conservatives as an alternative to the Liberal government. My constituents are not prepared to accept them as an alternative, and I am convinced that the people of Canada are not prepared to accept them as an alternative unless they are prepared to add to the policy as we see it, by giving their support, not to a negative amendment, but to a positive one which we have when we take the Conservative amendment amended by ours.
I am satisfied-and I know hon. members across the way will not like this-that this government does not enjoy the confidence of the people. In fact, I would not have to spend much time looking into the crystal ball to satisfy myself that a 1947 election could well result in the virtual annihilation of the Liberal party.
Oh, oh.

I said that was my personal conviction, and any interjections that come from the political wilderness on the opposite side of the house will not change that personal conviction at all. Everywhere in the country the government is being accused of being unable to shake off the war complex. Personally I think that is a legitimate charge.
While most Canadians, in my opinion, recognize the continuing necessity of certain controls, they are charging the government with the maintenance of certain ridiculous controls and regulations which are stifling production and distribution. I believe there is ample reason for arriving at that conclusion. For example, it reminds me of something that took place back home. Here is a great locker system with over SCO lockers. The farmers own these lockers. A farmer butchers his own animals. In the first place, he cannot get all of his meat into his locker. I presume he has to get rid of it by bootlegging it or selling it on the black market. I am not saying he does that, but I am. saying it may happen. The boards will not grant to that institution a slaughtering permit in order that one farmer who butchers more than he requires may sell part of it to another fellow who owns a locker. It reminds me of something I read the other day. It was said that inspectors from the wartime prices and trade board swiooped down on the farmer's house and they said to him, "Where in the world did you get all the meat?" He said, "Well, I found it necessary to butcher the whole animal at one time." There is a lesson in that.
It is asserted by many people in this country that the financial policy of this government has resulted in a national debt of staggering proportions. It takes no imagination to know that. This debt commands an annual interest tribute almost equal to our total national expenditures of ten years ago, and they look upon it as being a tragic situation. That is the reason they will, I was going to say-this is a bit crude-boot you fellows just about as far as you can go unless you mend your ways. I say it is a rather crude expression. I do not like to use it, but I think hon. members will agree with me that it is highly descriptive.
My next reason may be called a subsection of the previous one. The tax burden which has been allowed to pyramid until today it threatens the economic structure of Canada stands as the greatest single guarantee, in my estimation, that more and more Canadians will sooner or later become serfs in what we commonly boast of as a free democratic Canada. All you have to do is to see what is happening. All across the country taxes are going up and up until today property becomes virtually a liability. I should like to give two more reasons why these people across the way will likely be defeated.

Go ahead.

Yes.
Do not boot us too far.

I just have two more points which I think are essential to my argument. Canadians have resented the reluctance on the part of the Canadian government to assist more substantially, or let us say substantially, because there is not much assistance, in the field of public education in order that we may ensure equality of opportunity and the maintenance and development of our public educational services in the country. Do not let anyone say that I am advocating that we take from the provinces control of their educational system. No; these are grants, we say, and that is what the Canadian people are asking for. In conclusion, is it any wonder that more and more rank and file Liberals across the country are crying, ''Let us return to true Liberalism." Is it any wonder that so many of the Liberal leaders are crying for a return to true Liberalism. I come from a Liberal family.
