Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) on his fine speech, and I agree entirely with the last sentence he used. There is something which worries me a lot, namely, the number of people who did not vote at the last byelections. If we take for instance the constituency of Parkdale we find that out of a total of 41,087 electors on the list there were 17,118 who did not vote, and the elected member secured 8,212 votes; meaning by that, that the number of those who did not vote exceeded the total vote cast for him by 8,906.
It was the same thing in Pontiac, where the total number of electors was 49,435 and those

who voted numbered 32,124; meaning by that, if I count the rejected ballots, that 17,002 did not vote, and the elected member secured 11,412 votes, which means that the excess of those who did not vote was 5,590.
In Richelieu-Vercheres the situation was different. The total number of electors was 25,718; the votes cast, 20,263, and the difference was 5,455, while the elected member secured 11,984 votes.
In Portage la Prairie the total number of electors was 16,535 and the total vote was 11,941, including rejected ballots; meaning by that, that those who did not vote numbered 4,594, while the elected member secured 4,805 votes.
To summarize, in Parkdale 17,118 did not vote, or approximately two-fifths; in Pontiac 17,002 did not vote, or more than one-third; in Richelieu-Vercheres 5,455 did not vote, or one-fifth; and in Portage la Prairie 4,594 did not vote, which meant more than one-fourth. The total of those who did not vote in the four by-elections was 44.169.
It is all the worse because these lists were made immediately before the election, which means that these people were not interested in any of the candidates although all the parties had candidates in the field. It is pitiful to consider that, because this indifference to dominion politics is quite alarming. It is as bad as what happened in France. In France the people were saying, "I don't care; it is the business of the politicians. Je m'en fous". "I don't care". The result was communism, social trouble, ruin, famine and despair.
It is important that the Canadian people be informed about dominion politics. They can get information in Hansard, but unfortunately the English press is lacking in that respect. The French press in this country is much more informative about dominion politics than the English press. The might before last I had a conversation with a big newspaperman wTho told me that the people did not care. Of course the people do not care, for a very good reason. They have no information, and they look at the funny sections of the press and read sensational reports about murders and other things like that.
The house has done a very good job since the beginning of the session. The members have worked hard and those who have spoken have done so very well. Some legislation has been passed and I give credit to my colleagues for that, but I find that very often the discussion is purely academic. There are some interruptions at times and some members express loudly their views, which are different from those of the speaker. It is natural. It is just a way of expressing oneself and telling

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
the speaker that one does not agree with him. Although I do not indulge in those practices, I understand them and am quite tolerant of them, and I try to be as kind to the house as the house is to me.
But the Canadian people, even those who are not informed by the press, read Hansard and know to some extent what is being done here, and they have respect for members of parliament individually. But I do not know whether they have great respect for our parliamentary institutions, and it is a question of great concern. One thing that is of great concern is that when they abandon their former political affiliations they try new groups and new parties. I understand that, because when they are not satisfied with the leadership of their party they do, like my hon. friend the member for Red Deer, join another party and try to make the best of it. But I will tell him that the main thing is to try to reform the Liberal party from within or from without, because the Liberal party has a background that is still popular, and the Liberal party can do something for the future of the country if we get rid of the obnoxious elements within it.
I have been very patient for fifteen years, but I cannot understand the idea of being more conservative than the Progressive Conservative party, more socialistic than the C.C.F., and more optimistic than the Social Credit party.
Peptimistic.

Optimistic. You know,
Mr. Speaker, there are strange things at times. Is it possible to have a government composed of men who have not the same ideals to govern this country? When that is the case, those who represent the real Liberal tradition have to make concessions to those belonging to another faith. Liberalism has been excellently defined by my hon. friend who has just spoken. Liberalism is the friend of the individual, the promoter of private initiative, and the defender of decentralization. These are all principles of the Liberal party, and, besides that, the policy of the Liberal party is supposed to be 100 per cent Canadian policy. It has not always been so, just because the party was catering to hon. gentlemen who lead the opposition. I fought them since Mr. Arthur Meighen was leader of the Conservative party. I fought them all. I fought Ferdinand the Bull. I was very well received by the house but I had no success. Why not? Because in this country there is a propaganda which is just as bad as the one in other parts of the British empire. In India, the Indians do not have the right to vote 83166-821
as citizens of India. They vote as Moslems or as Hindus. They vote according to their religion. In Palestine they vote according to their race. Here in Canada we have a racial problem. On one side we have those who say that they are British, and of course they see everything from the British point of view; there are others who are like the negroes of the south. No question is considered objectively, and I regret that very much.
What did we gain in the international policies of the world? There were promises made to us. We had the promise that Mr. Pearson, who apparently is an able man, would be secretary of the united nations organization. He was not. But we had compensation. We were told that we would be on the security council. But we were not there. That was another disillusionment. Afterwards we were told we were to dictate the peace to Germany. We were not invited there any more than we were invited to Teheran. As Mr. Cardin so well said, we should not be sorry about it because we had no reason to be there since we were not invited to Moscow. But still we go on, and some members on all sides of the house are offended because we are not invited. We are invited when we have gifts, but when we have no gifts we are not invited.
During the war, and even last year I was often alone in standing against the financial policies of the government; they were absurd policies, destructive of the wealth of the nation. You know very well, Mr. Speaker, that when the tap on the lower floor is wide open, the tap upstairs does not run so freely. We were giving money freely to all the nations of the world-Great Britain, France and other nations-while our own people were still suffering. In front of my office today I saw notice of a meeting of the world health conference. Think of that! Yet in this country there are poor people who are sick and -who have no help at all; but they are Canadians. We wall look after those from other countries first. I am sorry about that, but there is a ray of hope everywhere and the ray of hope is that in the near future I trust the burden of taxation will be so heavy that those who have racial differences of opinion in prosperity will come close together in adversity to oppose that burden. Perhaps that will be the only good effect of the heavy taxation which is being imposed on this country. If it brings good understanding amongst good Canadians it will have served a good purpose. But I am not in favour of high taxation.
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

Something which does not exist in this house but which exists in this country is a strong Canadian feeling, the desire to promote Canada and to raise it from the small country that it is now to one of the biggest countries in the world. That will be done by trade. It frill not be done by ambassadors some of whom are just the butlers of the British ambassadors. It will be done by true Canadian ambassadors who are promoting Canadian interests throughout the world, ambassadors of good will to promote trade; and I do not mean the trade of Santa Claus, exports that we pay for ourselves from the taxes that we collect from the Canadian people, but real bargaining, real trading and perhaps real bartering if the money scheme we have under the Bank of Canada or the one which my hon. friends of the Social Credit party are expounding is without any good results. We must have trade. We must have economic independence; and if it is impossible to have economic independence without political independence, let us have them both and let Canada go forward while Great Britain is on her decline.
We had a sad performance with regard to the Canadian flag. In 1945 I said that it was too soon to have a flag of our own and that if we were a colonial country, as Canada is now, instead of a truly Canadian flag, we should have a union jack larger than the one of standard size. But times have changed during the last year or two, since that was said in the house, precisely on account of the burden of taxation. We see important bodies like the chamber of commerce, boards of trade and other institutions coming to the government and insisting on a reduction in taxes. As I once said to the leader of the C.C.E. party, those who voted for the loan-gifts cannot complain about taxes, but I can. Those who voted against the gift can complain against taxation, but those who voted for it cannot, without being called illogical.
What we need in this country is a truly Canadian flag. We need a Canadian anthem. I am very sorry to see that somewhere in the west some men were arrested by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police precisely because they were calling for "0 Canada" as the national anthem. There was some protest by some friends of mine. I have one here in my hand. How is it that in this country men are put in gaol by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police because they insist on singing "0 Canada?"
I still have hope for the future, but my mind is not satisfied; and I have been fighting

for a long time to try to awaken the government, to try to open their eyes, telling them that the more Canadian the government is, the more popular it will be because of the response of the Canadian people who are eager to see this country the greatest in the whole world.
Mr. SMITH (Calgary West); Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Where was it that the people were put in gaol by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police because they sang "0 Canada"?

I will read the letter which was sent by a friend of mine, Mr. John R, Spendlove, addressed to the R.C.M.P., "C" division, Place d'Armes, P.O. building, Montreal. The letter refers to civil investigation bureau, divisional file No. 41M269-3518, HQ file No. 41D 269-3D178. I intended to make a shorter speech, but if hon. members desire to have this letter read I will put it on record.
Read it.
I merely asked where it was.

The letter reads:
Dear Sir:
(Inspector N. Courtois)
Your letter of March 7 received, and I was favourably impressed by the way your Constable Racine carried out orders which impress me most unfavourably.
If it is wrong to express a preference for "O Canada" as our national anthem, why do you not investigate and start a file on our world champion skaters, for whom "0 Canada" was played by bands in foreign cities as our national anthem ?
In many cases the mere fact of the R.C.M.P. calling on a person and starting a file on him, would hurt him greatly. In my ease, living at home, it has not injured me.
I am a war veteran, volunteer, and I resent being investigated and having a file started on me for expressing my admiration for two courageous persons who had the audacity, the impertinence, to state that they were Canadian citizens, not British subjects, and that their national anthem was "0 Canada."
I suggest that the person responsible for this crazy order come to Montreal and investigate the theatre managers who play "0 Canada" as our national anthem in their theatres.
In his covering letter to me this gentleman also says:
I had written the R.C.M.P. officer in charge "K" division, Edmonton, asking the address of and expressing admiration for two men, Messrs. Boreen and Henry, who insisted forcibly, that since "0 Canada" was our anthem and that they

The Address-Mr. Hazen
were Canadian citizens, a certain orchestra must play "0 Canada." They were sentenced to a fine and jail. This was some months ago.
You know, sir, this is pitiful. I understand that it did not happen in the city represented by my hon. friend who interrupted me, but this is a disgrace to our country.
I shall explain why I intend to vote against the two amendments. In the first place, I cannot understand the meaning and purpose of the Social Credit amendment at this time, any more than I could on other occasions. That may be a deficiency on my part. I see a lot about production; I see a lot about purchasing, but I do not see anything about distribution, which is the link between production and purchasing. I would say to my hon. friends of the Social Credit party with all due respect that they remind me of newlyweds who, on the day of their marriage, are given a beautiful car by their parents. Some friends attach old cans and old shoes to the back of the car, which make a lot of noise and stir up a lot of dust. These are the theories of the Social Credit party. It is unfortunate, but that is my belief.
If I may be permitted to say a word about * the amendment of the official opposition, my point of view is that, while I have a soft spot in my heart for my Liberal colleagues, the policies of all parties are alike and they all vote together on the main issues. Therefore I do not understand -why any opposition group should run an opposition candidate against a supporter of the government in any by-election or even at the next general election, because they all vote together. I warned them time and again that such policies were dangerous; they all voted for them. They all voted together; they all shook hands. I suffered a personal insult when the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), held out an olive branch to the Liberal party and said we should all come together. Has the Liberal party fallen so low as to be asked to unite with the Tory party? It is an insult, to me; it is a slap in the face, and I am greatly surprised that the matter has not been referred to by anyone before this time. Since all parties have voted together, and since the Liberal party has been wrong in following the advice, the wrong advice, the pernicious advice given by Mr. Hanson and all the leaders of the Tory party, I do not see how the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) can rise in his place in this house and say, "We do not have confidence in you. We have no confidence because you have promoted our policies." This is the reason I have voted against the policies of the government; because they were Tory policies,
policies to appease the Tory leader of the opposition. As a Liberal I stood against them, and I am still against them. It would be absurd for me to support the amendment of the leader of the opposition, any more than I could support the subamendment of the Social Credit party.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in this debate, but in view of certain articles appearing in a New Brunswick newspaper which reached me yesterday, one of which I intend to quote to the house, I deem it my duty to bring to the attention .of the government a situation which has recently developed at the port of Saint John, and which may adversely affect its welfare and is of deep concern to its citizens. I believe this matter is also of importance to the port of Halifax, since it may affect shipping through both these Atlantic ports when the seaports of the St. Lawrence river are locked in ice.
The matter to which I refer is the diversion of cargo ships from Canadian ports, either Saint John or Halifax, to the United States port of Portland to load grain for shipment overseas. A press dispatch from Portland last week announced the diversion of these ships. I know of no better or more succinct way of bringing this matter to the attention of the government than by quoting from an editorial which appeared in the Telegraph-Journal, published in the city of Saint John, under date of last Saturday, In passing, I may say that this newspaper does not support his Majesty's loyal opposition but is independent in politics. The editorial is headed, "Canadian ports must fight this threat", and reads as follows:
The chairman of the port committee of Portland, Maine, announced yesterday that 4,000,000 bushels of Canadian grain would be shipped through liis city in the next month.
A dispatch quotes him as saying that he and the Portland chamber of commerce had offered "to assist Canada in a shipping emergency caused by the box car shortage" and had approached the dominion government, which had; promptly assigned three ships to Portland to load for Europe.
Now. nobody can blame this gentleman and his associates for trying to drum up business for-their own port, but the federal government is to be condemned in the strongest terms for accepting this "kind assistance." The grain that is sent through Portland obviously won't be sent through Saint John or Halifax. That means that Canadians will lose work and wages to which they are entitled-and lose them to the labourers of a foreign country.
We have been through all this before-the rivalry between Canadian ports and those of the United States. In central Canada there seems to have been a long-time conspiracy to deprive our waterfront workmen of a livelihood.
The Address-Mr. Hazen

Our people fought this once, and beat it, and they must stand ready to fight it now and in future if the ports of Saint John and Halifax are to survive. The Portland shipments, transparently disguised as an emergency, must be viewed in their true light as an underhand effort again to divert to United States competitors the trade on which our existence depends.
The threat is serious and real.
If there are box cars to carry grain to Portland, there are box cars to carry it to Saint John and Halifax, The saving in mileage as between Portland and Saint John is too trifling to be considered and certainly does not constitute a valid excuse for the double-dealing aimed in our direction.
At the very hour when the announcement Was being made in Portland, we had ships waiting in our harbour, unable to get grain. They were losing time and money-a situation not calculated to promote increased traffic for this port- and the official explanation was that box cars weren't available to bring grain here.
No box car3 to bring grain here! But box cars to carry 1,000,000 bushels to Portland, where the first of three ships is to start taking on Canadian grain cargo Monday! No situation could be more ridiculous or unfair, and if Ottawa expects us to put up mildly With treatment of this kind it gravely misjudges the temper of this part of Canada.
Back in 1931, the famous English port authority, Sir Alexander Gibb, was brought to the dominion by the federal government to make a survey of national ports. He found that Saint John and Halifax had suffered heavily from "the actual diversion of great quantities of Canadian grain to United States ports."
Sir Alexander said in his report:
"Apart from sentiment and patriotism, there are moral and national, as well as some sound business grounds, for the maritimes claim that the grain trade, which is already in many ways subsidized by dominion funds, should utilize to a greater extent the facilities that have been established for it at a considerable expenditure of dominion money."
The sentimental, patriotic, moral, national and business grounds are the same today as in 1931.
And the dominion government must be compelled to recognize them!
During the war years, when our transportation systems were taxed to the limit no situation of this kind arose, and an explanation is called for as to why such a situation should develop nearly two years after the war in Europe has ended.
When the war was on we heard no complaint of a lack of box cars. Evidently there were enough cars to do the job, and a big job it was. An explanation is needed as to why there is a car shortage at the present time. Box cars must have been built during the war years and in increasing numbers since the war has ended to replace those that were worn out and to increase the number in use. It is not unreasonable to ask how those cars are being used.

If the coal strike in the United States last summer or the seamen's strike on the great lakes was the cause of a lack of grain coming to our elevators on the Atlantic coast this winter, a complete explanation of the matter should be furnished by the government.
The government should give a. satisfactory explanation, if it has one to give, of how grain could be moved from the prairies to Portland, Maine, when it could not be moved from the prairies to the port of Saint John or the port of Halifax. What the people of my constituency want to know is this: Does the dominion government intend to divert trade permanently from Canadian Atlantic ports during the winter season to United States ports? The editorial from the Telegraph-Journal which I have quoted says:
The Portland shipments, transparently disguised as an emergency, must be viewed in their true light as an underhand effort again to divert to United States competitors the trade on which our existence depends.
Is it the policy of the government to divert Canadian trade to United States ports, or is there merely a transfer of three ships to Portland, Maine, to meet an unusual and temporary situation? If this is the' start of a new policy, it will have to be fought. Cana- ' dians must see to it that Canadian goods are shipped through Canadian ports.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) stated, at the conclusion of his remarks, that the reason he was going to vote against the social credit amendment was that he was still unable to understand what was involved in the amendment as well as in the social credit proposals. He claimed that he did not understand them any better today than he did ten years ago. The only remark I would care to make with regard to what he alleges as his reason is that "a man persuaded against his will is of the same opinion still."
I feel that the situation in this chamber as at present constituted is not conducive to the acceptance of new ideas. I think it has been quite evident for many years that, regardless of how sound the proposals are that may be advanced in opposition quarters, it is rarely the case that they are accepted by the government in power. All of which leads me to the conclusion that our political system is due for a change if democracy is to function more effectively. My personal feeling is that, so far as the results to the Canadian people are concerned, what we witness here from year to year is largely a farce. It makes no difference what the government brings down in the way of legislation, we

The Address-Mr. Kuhl
know beforehand the government supporters are going to support it. It makes very little difference how many arguments are advanced by the opposition with respect to what they consider defects or improvements, for very few changes are made. So the conduct of the business of this house resolves itself largely into one of jockeying for political advantage. Consequently I feel that the time has arrived when some radical changes will have to be made before the people of Canada enjoy a genuine democracy. I am gratified personally to observe that there is a movement on foot in this country which, when it reaches full fruition, will, I think, bring about the necessary parliamentary reform. I do not believe that the people of any country can obtain the results which they unitedly desire under a political party system. I feel that the political party system has outlived its usefulness and must be supplanted by a new system.
What would you suggest?

I intend to suggest an alternative before I conclude my remarks. What I am saying now is in criticism and comment on the remark provoked by a statement by the hon. member for Temiseouata.
It is my purpose to confine my remarks largely to the last section of the amendment moved by the leader of my group, but, before I do so, there are one or two general remarks which I should like to make with respect to the first sections of that amendment. I feel that these sections have been adequately and ably dealt with by my colleagues who have preceded me and anything I wish to say upon them is merely for emphasis and for personal gratification.
I believe that my colleagues have diagnosed the economic ills of this country correctly, and that the remedy which they have proposed is the proper one. Notwithstanding everything that is said to the contrary, I believe that the debate has definitely indicated that our troubles are largely if not entirely confined to monetary policy. All reforms I believe wait on monetary reform. I am quite convinced that the only manner in which the trend toward centralization of power and control not only in this country but throughout the entire world can be halted and eliminated is through monetary reform. The first section of the social credit amendment I believe indicates this fact when it urges "the return to parliament of complete and effective control of Canada's financial policy".
Section 91 of the British North America Act gives the dominion parliament exclusive authority over the matter of money, all money,
in the nation. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) argued that we had complete control at the present time, or at least that the control was vested in parliament but that it was not exercising that control in the interests of the people. On that point I quite agree with him. I consider that the piecemeal surrender of the crown's highest prerogative, that of creating and issuing all the money of the nation, is one of the most wicked deeds that has been perpetrated in this nation of ours. I have previously quoted that great American statesman, Abraham Lincoln, upon the significance of the crown's prerogative of creating and issuing the money of the nation. I wish to repeat what he said, because I feel that it is the most important aspect of our national economy that can be considered. I am positively amazed, I am shocked, to observe the attitude not only of members of this house but of many people outside when one refers to the fact that the government should be the sole issuer of the money of the nation, or that it is advisable or desirable for the government to be the issuer of the money of the nation. Immediately that is suggested, you hear people on every side make remarks about funny money, rubber money, printing press money, and kindred remarks. That is a tragedy to me, because it indicates that we have drifted so far away from what constitutes the rights of the people that we are calling that which is wrong right. Today there are many who look upon the state issuing of money with suspicion, whereas actually the state should be the only authority to issue in the original instance all the money of the nation. But we have descended to the point where today the vast majority of the money, one might as well say all the money of the nation, is created and issued in the original instance by private individuals. I consider that one of the grossest crimes which have been committed in this nation. Abraham Lincoln said this:
The government should create, issue, and circulate all the currency and credit needed to satisfy the spending power of the government and the buying power of consumers. The privilege of creating and issuing money is not only the supreme prerogative of the government, but it is the government's greatest creative opportunity. The people can and will be furnished with a currency as safe as their own government. Money will cease to be the master, and will become the servant of humanity. Democracy will rise superior to the money power.
Surely that is of great importance. I do not think there should be any question whatsoever of the desirability of the government being the creator and the issuer of the money of the nation. It should be taken for granted that
12S4
The Address-Mr. Kuhl

the creating and the issuing of all money in the original instance is the prerogative of the crown. But that prerogative has been surrendered piecemeal- over a long period of time to private individuals, and that should never have been permitted to come about. As a consequence of this betrayal, and I consider it a betrayal, of public trust we have reached the position referred by my colleague the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), where the people of this country are almost submerged in public debt, public debt which is absolutely inexcusable and unnecessary. I say, sir, that a national debt -in this country is a national lie. It should never have been permitted- to arise in the first place. If successive governments of the past had been faithful to the sacred trust -reposed in them we would never have had to submit to a national debt; for a country, any country, whether it be Canada, the United States or any other which is rich in resources, rich in skill and knowledge on the part of -its people to process those resources into finished products, does no-t require a national debt. The alarming feature in this situation for the future is that some day this inexcusable situation will be made the excuse for depriving the people -of this country of what little liberty they still enjoy.
We saw what happened in the old dominion of Newfoundland as a consequence of that debt-creating policy. At one time they enjoyed the privilege of electing their own parliament. Today they are without a parliament. Their parliament was dismissed and substituted for -it was a financial dictatorship. The reason given was that the people were unable to manage their own affairs. We had an argument similar to that in Canada prior to the war, and no doubt within a few years it will be raised again. There was an argument abroad that we had too much government in Canada. Ten governments were too much, too expensive, a luxury that we could not afford, and there was an agitation to attempt to eliminate the provincial governments and concentrate all control in the central government. That is certainly a totalitarian trend and I am fearful that, if this debt-creating policy is allowed to continue, before long we shall again be confronted with such an agitation.
If the governments of the past had been faithful to their trust and had not surrendered to the private banking institutions the crown's highest prerogative we would not today be witnessing the dominion-provincial controversy which has been going on for some considerable time. I believe that the difficulties which the dominion and the provinces are

now involved in would have been largely obviated, if not completely, if the central government had remained faithful to its trust. So far as the controversy itself is concerned, I wish to make -this comment. I believe that the dominion government is completely in the wrong -and that the provinces are completely in the right. I feel that the dominion is adopting a dog-in-the-manger attitude in the controversy. The dominion government refused to eat the hay which they have themselves; they will not allow the provinces to eat it, and- they are seeking to filch from the provinces what little hay they have. That certainly can be characterized as a dog in the manger attitude.
&o far as any solution is concerned, with respect to rearranging tax fields, I am sure it must occur to any person who reasons logically that there can be no solution by merely rearranging the tax field, because in the final analysis it is the same set of taxpayers who foot the bill whether the provinces collect the taxes or -the dominion collects them. I am not going to make any comments concerning the nature of the tax agreements. I think there are more vital issues involved. What I object to mostly in the arrangements that are being made is the -trend toward centralization in the central government, which certainly means the loss of freedom to the provinces. It is the duty of the dominion government to exercise the crown's highest prerogative not only in the interests of governing the country from the point of view of the dominion government but also in the interests of the provinces themselves.
If the dominion exercised its prerogative the provinces could be kept continuously supplied with all the financial assistance they need to enable their people to enjoy the standard of living which is physically possible. I know that when we speak of the need of national money or the advisability of national money there are those who immediately consider that we are advocating something for nothing. That is totally wrong. We are aware of the fact that our government can no more give something for nothing than the individual can. When the national government or any other government issues money for public services it is doing nothing less than monetizing the wealth of the country. That should be done to the extent that wealth is not monetized through the regular channels of business. That raises the basic contention that we of this group have constantly made, namely that industry does not monetize the whole of the production. There is always a shortage of money with respect to the price value of goods and, consequently, when the

The Address-Mr. Kuhl
national government steps in and uses national money to finance old age pensions or pensions for the blind, or uses it to finance public works it is doing nothing less than monetizing the unmonetized portion of national wealth. As a consequence of so doing, taxation could be reduced; in fact it could be reduced to the point where taxation was absolutely unnecessary.
The last section of the social credit amendment calls for redefining and clarifying the constitutional rights and responsibilities of dominion and provincial governments, together with the adoption of scientific formulae for alloting to the provinces sufficient revenues to enable them fully to discharge their responsibilities without increasing the tax burden already borne by their people. If the dominion government were to exercise its right of creating and issuing all the money of the nation I do not think there would be very much of a problem with respect to redefining and clarifying the constitutional rights of the provinces and the dominion. Nevertheless there are doubtless some things which will have to receive attention; certainly it may involve constitutional amendment. I am not suggesting that they will or that they will not. One thing I am sure of is that if the provinces are to be left with the financial resources that they have under the British North America Act they will be unable to meet the obligations which they are in duty bound to carry out under the terms of that act. It will be impossible for the provinces to discharge their respective responsibilities without some additional aid. That may involve constitutional amendments, and should steps be taken in future, through a conference either of the provinces, or a combination of the provinces, and the dominion to redefine the constitutional position of the country, there are some things which I should like to say about that situation.
I believe that the constitutional circumstances of this country are such that they demand to be dealt with in a far broader manner than is generally suggested by students of constitutional affairs in Canada. I am not at this time going to enter into all the arguments I have presented on past occasions in this house on this particular subject. I do not wish to repeat, but because this subject is coming more to the fore all the time, and will become more important as time goes on, I must once again record my decided disapproval of the present circumstances and indicate what I believe must be done to rectify them.
I think it is quite inconsistent of us to go abroad in the world and preach from the 83166-83
housetops our faith in democratic principles and then come back home and ignore and ride roughshod over the rights of citizens, as has been done for some considerable time in this country. I wish to say, with respect to any clarifying or redefining of constitutional powers in Canada, that the only alteration to which I will give my approval and consent is one which involves a completely new constitution. I believe that the people of the country must be consulted where their fundamental rights are concerned, and in this question I feel that their fundamental rights are being ignored, disregarded and overlooked.
As I said, I do not wish to repeat all the arguments I have presented in the past as to the reasons why I advocate and urge a completely new constitution, but this I must say and repeat, that it is my firm belief that Canada has no constitution. I know that statement is always received with much scoffing, but it is true. I have argued in the past, with much evidence to substantiate the contention, that the people of Canada did not have the privilege, until December 11, 1931, of creating a constitution of their own.
I believe that adequate evidence can be brought to bear to substantiate the fact that the British North America Act was never a constitution but merely an imperial statute used to govern a colony, and it was not until December 11, 1931, through the statute of Westminster, that the control over the Canadian people was relinquished by the British people so that Canadians might establish their own constitution. That was done, I firmly believe, through the statute of Westminster. The provinces of Canada must essentially enjoy their sovereignty before they can consummate a federal union. They were not sovereign prior to 1931 and the statute of Westminster made them sovereign in order that they might federate in the manner that the fathers of confederation intended but were not permitted to do.
Since December 11, 1931, no steps have been taken to consummate an agreement in this country between the provinces, to be ratified by the people later; and, since a federal union is a union of sovereign states mutually agrees ing to adopt a constitution, I assert that there is no federal union and can be no federal union. There is no constitution in this country and cannot be until the provinces sign an agreement which is submitted to the people of Canada for ratification.
I challenge anyone in Canada to produce anything in the nature of an agreement between the provinces, which was ratified by the people of Canada, and therefore I ask,

The Address-Mr. Kuhl

how can anyone assert that the Canadian people have a constitution when they have agreed to none?
I have had the right and privilege, along with my fellow Canadians, since December 11, 1931, to be consulted on the matter of a constitution. I have not been consulted, and I assert therefore, as I have asserted before, that as a citizen of this country, until I along with the majority of my fellow citizens have the right to mark a ballot either in favour of or against the constitution of the country, there can be no constitution.
I am not in favour of a state of anarchy continuing, which I contend is the position legally in this country. I want to see the circumstances rectified in the interests of all the people, and I want to see it done democratically. I have on previous occasions read evidence of the special committee on the British North America Act, in 1935, in which I quoted authorities who indicated how this constitutional position could be rectified. I say that, unless some action is taken, serious circumstances may presently develop in this country.
I have asserted that the only governing authorities with any legal power in this country are the nine provinces, and they have not thus far surrendered their authority. As a consequence of that position, there is developing in western Canada a new movement known as the western Canada federation, which has for its object the setting up of a federation of western provinces. I have here the prospectus which they issued. The president of the organization is John Evans, a resident of Saskatchewan since 1892, honorary president of the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, who was at one time a member of this house for the constituency of Rosetown-Biggar, from 1921 to 1930. This western Canada federation proposes extending the boundarj' lines of the four western provinces up to the arctic circle. Personally, I do not think it is necessary to go to that extent to get justice on this question in Canada. I do not want to see this country Balkanized or divided up any more than anyone else does; but unless those who are responsible are going to do something to endeavour to straighten out this situation, such a thing will come about. I wish to say right here that if the people of western Canada as a majority desire to do this thing, if they wish to set up a western federation and create their own constitution, make their own laws and operate as a separate entity in this dominion, there is absolutely no legal power in the world, in this country or any-

where else which can stop the people of western Canada from doing that. In>
my opinion they have the absolute legal right to consummate a western Canada federation if thejr wish to do so.
Again I am not saying that I am in favour of dividing the west from the east, but this constitutional controversy is a burning issue in this country. I have done my level best to suggest ways and means by which it can be settled in the interest of all sections of Canada, but thus far there has been very little support in this house. I am satisfied that, as more of the people of Canada become acquainted with the constitutional position in this country, they will demand that appropriate action be taken. As I indicated at the commencement of my remarks, the only clarification and redefining of the constitutional issue to which I will lend my support is that which involves a completely new constitution. Whether that will be along the lines of the British North America Act or any other act is for the constituent assembly to say. One thing is imperative, and that is that the people shall have a voice in creating that constitution and shall be consulted personally and individually. Until such time as such an agreement is reached between the provinces and ratified by the people of Canada I assert, sir, that our constitutional position is a disgrace to an intelligent people.
In conclusion, I merely wish to say this. We have gone abroad in the world to proclaim our faith in democracy, in the freedom of the individual, in the rights of the individual citizen. That is good. But I suggest that, before we attempt to run the rest of the world, before we seek to tell other nations how to conduct themselves, we first put our own house completely in order. Before we complain about the violation of the rights of other people in the world, let us make sure that the rights of our own people are observed. In short, let us remove the beams from our owm eyes before we seek to remove the motes from the eyes of others.

Mr. Speaker, I had prepared a modest address in which I intended to express my views in regard to the condition of the country and to advise the government what they should do about it. I had no intention whatsoever of entering into an acrimonious discussion with the Social Crediters until I was dragged into 83166-831
it by the references made to a speech of my own by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw).

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And a very fine speech it was.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It was an excellent speech; and if the hon. member for Red Deer had read it all, he would have made a better speech. I hope I do not have to apologize to the house for having spoken to a resolution in 1935 in which the phrase "social credit" was used. Of course at that time it did not have the same opprobrium it now' has. I wish to first explain to the house that when we used the phrase "social credit" we meant something; and what we meant was not a nostrum for everything which might happen to modern civilization. We used it as a social fact, and this is that fact, the credit which accrues as a result of the association of the people working together, or as a result of collective production, is as sound a basis for credit as the capital equipment of a capitalist w'hich he hypothecates at the bank for assistance to carry on his business.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is entirely right.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That was the meaning we had in using it. Now, sir, in order to justify the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), and in order also to show that the view's I expressed on the occasion referred to by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) are the views I shall express tonight and the views I have expressed as long as I can remember, here are some quotations from the same speech which my hon. friend omitted to give. I refer to page 2325 of Hansard for April 2, 1935:
Let me turn now, sir, to a brief summary of the economic situation in relation to purchasing power. Goods manufactured and sold at a profit cannot be bought back with the wages paid those who have produced them.
And further:	f
The fact that those who are employed do not receive and never have received sufficient income under the profit system to buy even the necessities of life, much less the entire output, together with the additional fact that machinery is displacing thousands from every industry, thus depriving a large percentage of the population of any income at all. has resulted in vast amounts of goods going to waste unused while millions are in want.
It w-as not because there was not enough money in existence, but because there was not enough money in the pockets of the consumers who would use the goods that had piled up, because the profits they should have used
The Address-Mr. Irvine

to buy the goods had gone into the pockets of those who operated the industry. I now turn to another section:
I am as firmly convinced as that I am in this house at this moment that if we are to attain prosperity we must plan our way, that our plans must be based upon economic truths and facts of the present time, and that such plans must be worked out by the application of established scientific principles.
I have one more quotation which will indicate to the house the circumstance and reason why we thought it would be of value if the social credit, in our interpretation of it, were loosened up at a moment when those who had money were afraid to invest it, and people were starving. We thought that, since they were starving and since they could produce goods, it was the business of the government to provide the necessary funds to put them to work at profitable industry. So we said:
We regard the problem chiefly as one of making available to the consumer enough purchasing power to equal the total prices of all commodities that are for sale, and we regard provision of the required amount of purchasing power as the most advisable next step, since it will bring about the immediate distribution of the goods required to satisfy the wants of the community and thus prevent revolution and give us time to think out succeeding steps in a fundamental economic and social reconstruction.
That was the reason we had such a motion, not by any means to follow the most extraordinary will-o'-the-wisp that has ever been projected into political discussion in this country, which has been advocated by my hon. friends to my left.
Now, sir, I turn to the speech I wish to deliver, and I may have to make a reference to the Social Credit party as I go along. I believe that the criticism or advice hon. members offer this administration should be based upon the actual situation, social, economic and political, which confronts us at the present moment. My first remark in that regard is that in my opinion, the morale of the Canadian people is extraordinarily low for a nation which has just emerged victorious in a great world war. That lower morale is not due to economic distress, because despite the fact that the cost of living is going up and unemployment is beginning to grow, the economic condition is still reasonably good in a comparative way.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, note the qualifications. A nation needs an inspiration to achieve its utmost, whether in war or in peace, and when war broke out the Canadian people needed a rallying point. I say to you, sir, that capital-
[Mr. Irvine.1
ism was bankrupt in providing that rallying point. I question very much whether the youth of Canada would have voluntarily responded to an appeal to fight for the capitalism which produced the conditions of 1932. So it was necessary for us to find a rallying cry that would call the nation, and "democracy" was that cry. Democracy was the rallying cry, and capitalism accepted it as an expedient. Capitalist leadership, I am convinced, when it adopted the rallying cry of democracy had no intention whatever of implementing democratic policies on the heels of victory. But the public still remembers, though it is not supposed to have a long memory. The public remembers the rallying cry; it remembers the sacrifices made in order that democracy might be made safe. So today the morale of our people is low because they are suffering from deep disappointment. They find that the steps necessary for launching out toward a democratic system of society have not been undertaken; thus they are disappointed.
Capitalist economics is void of the elements of the democratic principle. My hon. friends of the Social Credit party have often argued that we have democracy in industry because the ballots of our consumers, which is the money with which they buy their needs, determine the nature of the market and the kind of goods the system will produce. Well, all you have to notice is the number of ballots some people have as compared with the number of ballots other people have. If in this house we were to suggest that a few hon. gentlemen should have a hundred votes while those of the common herd have one vote each, not very many of us would stand for that sort of thing. Yet in the economic world there are privileged individuals who can mark a thousand ballots in the economic market for every one the ordinary man can afford to use.
I wish to point out briefly what economic democracy means to me as the thing that Canada needs most at the moment and that her people are expecting, because, as I have said, we fought for that ideal. We would not have fought for capitalism; yet now we are seeing capital institutions reconstructed and reinvigorated, without any real- effort to establish the principles of democracy.
Economic democracy implies, first of all, the collective ownership of such means of life as must be used by everybody but which it is not possible for everyone privately to own. However, when the essential means of life of a community are owned by an individual or a corporation, the position of that community

The Address-Mr. Irvine
is one of dependence upon such individual or corporation for its very life. It may be the case that the corporation, without regard for the needs of the community and in order to maintain its profit rate, may deliberately choose to curtail the volume of production. The community then must necessarily suffer. That is the situation today, and that is undemocratic.
Second, economic democracy implies a common purpose to which every basic industry as well as every part of the industrial mechanism must be geared in order that we may utilize the natural resources, man-power, plant and equipment, science and technical skill to the end of achieving full production for peace as we did in war.
Third, economic democracy implies social planning to achieve a collective purpose. Shall we undertake democratically to plan, that is, as a community, just as a corporation now plans for its profits under an economic dictatorship, disguised under the attractive dress of so-called political democracy?
Fourth, economic democracy also implies the finding of the ways and means of distributing the national income more equitably in keeping with the demands of the farmers for parity prices and those of organized labour in terms of a living wage.
Fifth, it implies devising and working out the technique of democratic management so that workers in industry will be permitted to participate in the direction and operations of industry, thus promoting harmonious relations and the exercise of democratic cooperation.
Such a programme is not only one which fits the times in which we live, but also one which is designed to implement the democratic objectives which we hold out for our people. If such a programme were to be seriously considered it would mean that we could solve such problems as housing, as the extension of our railroad building, as the building of highways, as the - undertaking of irrigation and reforestation projects, town planning and all other things necessary for a higher type of life. But of course the question will be raised by the government, as it has been in all my experience, as to there not being sufficient money for any such projects as I have been suggesting would be implied in instituting real economic democracy.
I am suggesting that we must finance peace in a manner similar to that which we used to finance war. The object of financing war was to get the greatest amount of war materials into the front line with the least possible waste of time. The objects of peace are
equally as clear; that is, to get into the stomachs of our people and on to the backs of our people the essentials of life as they are required both in time and in quantity. I know there are big industrialists who oppose financing peace as we financed war, and that is not difficult to understand. In financing war they were doing it at a very good profit. Our war materials were destroyed on the battle lines and nothing was left as a backlog to interfere with the consuming market. Indeed I believe it is right to say that War Assets Corporation has spent much of its time in trying to steer some of these surplus goods away from the consumer market into the hands of the dealers or the trade, as it is called.
The capitalists of our time welcome large loans by this country to other countries which will enable them to buy Canadian made goods because such loans increase or maintain prices at home. But if they were asked how they would feel if we were to finance great industrial projects in Canada by the use of our national credit without interest charges in order to supply our own consuming public at home, they would oppose that because such a process might interfere with their rate of profit.
If the policy which I have suggested were to be adopted we would have to find ways and means of distributing the abundance which would result to the consumers of Canada. We would have to devise a financial mecahnism to be used within our own borders comparable with the lend-lease system which was used internationally during the war to distribute war materials to various nations of the world. That financial mechanism would mean that an adequate income would have to be provided to the Canadian people to buy the output of industry. That income would have to be provided by increased wages and increased prices to farmers. It would have to be brought about by increasing pensions to the old people, to the blind, to the disabled and to the sick, and providing allowances to those who are not in a position to earn their own living. By taking them all together, we might be able to equate our consuming programme with our producing programme and thus carry on a constructive economic system.
To the extent to which the government is implementing such policies, it will be judged to be a failure or a success. Some say that our government is an entire failure. I would not go that far because I do not think any government was ever a failure in everything. I think this government has done many things very well, but I think it has failed to do the big things which, in turn, affect all the little things that go to make up the democratic way of life.
The Address-Mr. Irvine

There is no government that will survive this period unless it can meet the demands of the times; no government will survive this period which has indecision as a method and middle-of-the-roadism as a policy. The times call for definite affirmation and for militancy. There is no future for any government which will condone or encourage capitalist government irresponsibility and cling to policies of privilege rather than to serving the common interests of the masses of the people.
What is the attitude of the other parties? The Social Credit party has committed itself to the profit motive, to free enterprise, to competition. In doing so, it is protecting the very sources of the evils which it is trying to get rid of. It has become the evangelical fundamentalist of economic reaction, and by its
The Address-Mr. Irvine

rampant militancy in this respect has placed itself to the right of the Progressive Conservative party. It agrees, however, that something is needed. It thinks that something is the single simple expediency of monetary reform. I do not believe, of course, that the prosperity and abundance of which they speak are so easily come by as that. The leader of the party owes it to himself; he owes it to his cause; he owes it to the country to bring down a bill setting forth what that particular reform is that he is talking so much about. I want to see nailed down- in legislation the extravagant claims of this propaganda; I want to see it nailed down to specific proposals.
I listened to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) today. He utters aphorisms about money as if he alone had received the Divine revelation with respect to that. He advocates the simplest self-evident truth with the ponderosity of a hippopotamus climbing a Christmas tree. Just because every loan creates a deposit, which everybody who knows anything about banking or money knows and has known for a long time that by no means proves that all the other tripe which he talked about is true.
